messages.subject: memory leak patched in auto-dif
messages.body_plain:
There was a memory leak in the base class
I implemented:

    op_vector_vari

It was holding onto a std::vector that itself
allocated memory.  So I replaced the
std::vector<vari*> with an array vari**
that I allocated in our arena.

I had to rewrite a bit of the log_sum_exp
function, which was the only subclass that
depended on it.

I've been considering a completely different design
for var/vari that removes the virtual chain()
function but requires an extra 8 bytes per
expression argument to store the adjoint
multiplier (so it's a wash for unary
operators and gets worse with higher arity).
It'll be faster -- tight loop rather than
virtual function applications.

- Bob

messages.subject: var decl rules changed
messages.body_plain:
I'm now disallowing constraints in variable
declarations inside of derived data and
derived parameters (and generated quantities)
blocks.  That means range constraints for int
and double and also any of the subtypes of
vector, row_vector, or matrix (that is,
pos_ordered, simplex, corr_matrix, cov_matrix).

I changed the existing BUGS models that are
plugged into the unit tests.  This was mainly
replacing

   derived parameters {
       double(0,) sigma;
       ...

with

   derived parameters {
       double sigma;
       ...

Other ones may need to be fixed in the same way before
they'll run.

I wanted to make it clear that these constraints
weren't being enforced anywhere -- you're on your
own with derived parameters and derived data
and generated quantities.

Feeding illegal values into distributions or
other functions still gets checked.

This does remove the constraint on writing
illegal derived parameters, which used to be
in place.  But that constraint was illusory as
it didn't stop the constrained variable from
taking on illegal intermediate values before being
written.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] plan for variables
messages.body_plain:
We'll have our regular mtg Wed noon, right?
A

On Dec 31, 2011, at 1:17 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> Here's my final (I hope) proposal for the Stan
> language variable declarations and statement blocks:
>
> --------------------------------
> data {
>  <declarations>
> }
> transformed data {
>  <declarations>
>  <statements_no_sampling>
> }
> parameters {
>  <declarations>
> }
> transformed parameters {
>  <declarations>
>  <statements_no_sampling>
> }
> model {
>  <statements>
> }
> derived {
>  <declarations>
>  <statements_no_sampling>
> }
> -----------------------------------
>
> <statements> is a sequence of statements, including
> sampling statements (y ~ foo(theta)) and assignment
> statments (y <- foo(theta)) and loops.
>
> <statements_no_sampling> eliminates sampling statements.
>
> In each block of statements, assignments are only
> allowed to be made to local variables and variables
> declared in the block.
>
> Statement blocks allow local variables to be declared as
> in a programming language.  For example, we'll allow
>
> {
>  double mu;
>  for (n in 1:N) {
>    mu <- x[n] * alpha + beta;
>    y[n] ~ normal(mu,1);
>  }
> }
>
> The log probability variable lp__ will only be
> available in transformed parameters (to allow
> Jacobians) and in the model.
>
> (1) Input will read all declared data.
>
> (2) sampling is defined over the declared parameters;
> they're read by the model each leapfrog step.
>
> (3) output will produce all of the parameters,
> transformed parameters and derived quantities (but
> not any local variables).
>
> I know Andrew liked this idea, but I think it's a
> really bad idea to have "y ~ foo(theta)" be ambiguous
> and act as "y <- r_foo(theta)" in one context and
> "lp__ += foo_log(y,theta)" in others.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: major include/using problems and <> vs. ""
messages.body_plain:
We need to rethink the way the usings and includes
are happening because they're being defined at way
too high a scope.

I didn't realize this before, but putting a using
in the namespace brings it into the whole namespace.

We want to limit includes and usings as much as
possible to avoid name clashes.  ALL of the code is
going to need to be reviewed for this problem,

and boy are my fingers tired.  There are over 25

the tests pass, and (b) fix the makefile so that
failing tests cause failure?

consistency.  We need to figure out the right way
to do this globally.

3.  I moved files like prob/distributions_foo.hpp
to either prob/distributions/foo.hpp
or just to prob/foo.hpp.

There's no need to mock up a directory structure in a
file name.  There's still some vestiges of my
earlier flatter structure around we should get rid of
in test names.

4.  We need more includes on a per-file basis.
Specifically, if we have an independent file
for include, it should include everything it needs.
We have massive problems as I indicated in the previous
mail with things just getting brought in at a very
high-level scope when it should be lower.

It'd be really great if Daniel, Matt and I could sit
down and work out how we want this to work.  I may
have the wrong end of things here.

One issue is the namespace for agrad operations. I'd
originally put these in their own namespace, which
means you can't write:

     z = stan::agrad::log_sum_exp(y).

original functions?  Otherwise, we'll need:

There's really no way to get around functions like

     boost::math::lgamma()

unless we want a shadow lgamma() in stan::maths, which
might make sense.

a.  Try to keep lines 80 characters or under if
possible -- it's hard to scan through them otherwise.

b.  if (cond) ...  OVER  if(cond) ...

do this for cpp for me automatically.  We can script
replacements perhaps and I'll change my emacses.  Here's
the magic juju:

http://lingpipe-blog.com/2006/07/28/spring-cleaning-lingpipe-with-pmd-and-fixcrlf-and-emacs/

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] plan for variables
messages.body_plain:
These labels are as good as any, I suppose, but we want to make it super-clear that:

"data" = input
"transformed data" = computed before compilation
"parameters" = updated every leapfrog step
"transformed parameters" = computations performed every leapfrog step
"model" = computations of log-posterior performed every leapfrog step
"derived" = computations and simulations performed at the end of every iteration

By the way, why can't we have sampling in the "derived" step?  Unless I'm misunderstanding, that would seem to make sense to me.  For example, that would be the place in the algorithm to do forward sampling of leaves and to simulate fake data, replicated data, etc.

A

On Dec 31, 2011, at 1:17 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> Here's my final (I hope) proposal for the Stan
> language variable declarations and statement blocks:
>
> --------------------------------
> data {
>  <declarations>
> }
> transformed data {
>  <declarations>
>  <statements_no_sampling>
> }
> parameters {
>  <declarations>
> }
> transformed parameters {
>  <declarations>
>  <statements_no_sampling>
> }
> model {
>  <statements>
> }
> derived {
>  <declarations>
>  <statements_no_sampling>
> }
> -----------------------------------
>
> <statements> is a sequence of statements, including
> sampling statements (y ~ foo(theta)) and assignment
> statments (y <- foo(theta)) and loops.
>
> <statements_no_sampling> eliminates sampling statements.
>
> In each block of statements, assignments are only
> allowed to be made to local variables and variables
> declared in the block.
>
> Statement blocks allow local variables to be declared as
> in a programming language.  For example, we'll allow
>
> {
>  double mu;
>  for (n in 1:N) {
>    mu <- x[n] * alpha + beta;
>    y[n] ~ normal(mu,1);
>  }
> }
>
> The log probability variable lp__ will only be
> available in transformed parameters (to allow
> Jacobians) and in the model.
>
> (1) Input will read all declared data.
>
> (2) sampling is defined over the declared parameters;
> they're read by the model each leapfrog step.
>
> (3) output will produce all of the parameters,
> transformed parameters and derived quantities (but
> not any local variables).
>
> I know Andrew liked this idea, but I think it's a
> really bad idea to have "y ~ foo(theta)" be ambiguous
> and act as "y <- r_foo(theta)" in one context and
> "lp__ += foo_log(y,theta)" in others.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] plan for variables
messages.body_plain:
> "data" = input
 > "transformed data" = computed before compilation
 > "parameters" = updated every leapfrog step
 > "transformed parameters" = computations performed every leapfrog step
 > "model" = computations of log-posterior performed every leapfrog step
 > "derived" = computations and simulations performed at the end of
every iteration

Right.

Also, every leapfrog step, constrained parameters have
their constraints and log absolute Jacobian determinants
applied.  Once per sample, there's an additional constraining
of parameters for output.

Partial derivatives only get calculated for parameters.

 > By the way, why can't we have sampling in the "derived" step?  Unless
 > I'm misunderstanding, that would seem to make sense to me.  For
 > example, that would be the place in the algorithm to do forward
 > sampling of leaves and to simulate fake data, replicated data, etc.

As to no sampling in derived blocks, it's just a matter
of notation.  I think it's too confusing to have

   y ~ foo(theta)

mean

   lp__ += log(d_foo(y,theta));

in the model and

    y <- random_foo(theta);

in derived quantities.  So users are now required to write
out the assignment (y <- random_foo(theta)) expicitly
for derived quantities.  So we can do the forward sampling
to simulate data.

Eventually, I'd like to write a proper forward-sample
compiler.  It would require all the upper parameters
to be fixed, so that every time we sampled, all the
parameters (in the usual sense) would be known.  A simple
case is sampling leaves of a directed graphical model.
With the compiler, the user could use the same model code
to do the simulations.

I know you (Andrew) like the overloading of sampling notation
(y ~ foo(theta)).  That's probably a CS/stats cultural
difference, as I find the overloading in standard stats
notation and in Bayesian practice very confusing.

I agree with you (Andrew) that writing "random_foo"
is tacky and that R/BUGS users will start writing "d_foo" and
"r_foo" by mistake.  I'll at least be able to catch that with
the compiler and flag the location of the problem.

Not much I can do about the tackiness.

 > These labels are as good as any, I suppose,

If you have better suggestions for the labels, bring
them on!  I'm not happy with "parameters" -- it
matches BUGS's usage, but it doesn't match statistics
conventions where for normal(y|mu,sigma), the mu
and sigma are "parameters" and y is "data".  Hierarchical
Bayes screws all this up, because you can
have normal(mu|mu_mu,sigma_mu) and normal(y|mu,sigma)
where mu is both a "parameter" and "data".  I sort
of like "knowns" and "unknowns", but it just doesn't
seem to scan in the notation.  Or "constants" and
"variables", but that's also at odds with statistical
convention because some of the "modeled data" are
treated like variables even though their value is
known.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] plan for variables
messages.body_plain:
The currently implemented notation for
sampling in the model is:

    y ~ normal(m,s);

For generating random variates, it'll be:

    y <- random_normal(m,s);

Would sim_normal(m,s) be clearer or sample_normal(m,s)?

The sampling notation compiles to:

    lp__ += normal_log(y,m,s);

The user can refer to the function normal_log(y,m,s)
the same way as they refer to functions like sqrt(t).

They also have access to the lp__ accumulator (but
only in the model part), so they could write:

    lp__ <- lp__ + normal_log(y,m,s);

which compiles to:

    lp__ = lp__ + normal_log(y,m,s);

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I patched Stan so that the output order for derived
params matches those for params.  The order I gave
last time was right, but it's row-major, not column
major.  So if we have a[2,2,2] the output order is

   a[1,1,1], a[1,1,2], a[1,2,1], a[1,2,2],
   a[2,1,1], a[2,1,2], a[2,2,1], a[2,2,2].

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Multiplying matrices: var and double
messages.body_plain:
You need to use stan::maths and stan::agrad matrix
functions.  They're there exactly because they
auto-promote double matrices to var matrices.  All
of the ops there are defined for all mixed types.

The bummer is that we lose all the template
expression goodness, like lazy evaluation of
intermediates.  At least all the really expensive
matrix operations like solving are with single-typed
matrices.

I asked the Eigen developers and they say it's
going to require some work on their side with traits
to get two differently typed matrices to work together.
So far, it's only possible with regular and complex,
but the same logic would work for regular and auto-dif.

- Bob

On 1/2/12 11:32 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
> We can't multiply Eigen matrices of double and var together. I found
> this out while trying to get the Wishart distribution to compile for
> vars.
>
> I just checked in tests for Wishart. Some of them fail. I'll get them
> to pass once we are able to multiply matrices together.
>
> Regarding the multiplication, thoughts on how to make multiplication
> work generally?
>

messages.body_plain:
> Fixed now, apparently.

I have no idea what's going on with
your linux system.  We're not seeing any
of these problems on clang++ or g++
on either Mac or Windows.

We're going to move to system-specific builds,
I think.

 > Except the variable tracking size limit
 > thing ...

Variable tracking is part of optimization.
Maybe this is partly why g++ takes FOREVER to
compile compared to clang++.

 >    EXCEPTION. parse error at file STDIN line 62 column 22
 >      d_b_0<- 0.0001 + sum(tau_b_0_like) / 2.0;
 >                       ^-- here

Thanks.  I just added a function signature
type-checking to the parser, and forgot to declare an
overloaded version of sum() for arrays.  You can
find these in src/stan/gm/function_signatures.hpp.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] specify truncated distributions
messages.body_plain:
Yes, that'll work just fine as long as the
bounds are themselves constant.  It's a bit
trickier if they're variable.

I went with the JAGS notation T(lb,ub),
but we don't have many of the cumulative
densities implemented, so it's not very general
yet.

- Bob

On 1/3/12 11:46 PM, Wei Wang wrote:
> Now I need to specify a truncated distribution, say a half normal, is
> it correct to first constrain the variable in the declaration part
> (when it is allowed) and then just give it a non-truncated
> distribution? Like the following
>
>     parameters {
>        double(0, ) beta;
>        ......
>     }
>
>     model {
>        beta ~ normal(0, 1);
>        ......
>     }
>
> Also what is the correct syntax to directly specify a truncated
> distribution. Bugs uses I(lb, ub), and Jags uses T(lb, ub).
>

messages.subject: triangle distribution problems + fmax, fabs
messages.body_plain:
I tested the uniform distribution, and it works
just fine into the corners with NUTS with or without
declared bounds (i.e., transforms) on the variable.
The untransformed case runs much more slowly, probably
due to smaller step sizes.

Untransformed variables (1K adapt, 1K samples):

       0%   2.5%    10%    25%    50%    90%  97.5%   100%
   0.0018 0.0244 0.0946 0.2430 0.4878 0.8843 0.9842 0.9989

Transformed variables (same conditions):

       0%   2.5%    10%    25%    50%    90%  97.5%   100%
   0.0029 0.0261 0.0988 0.2770 0.5281 0.8961 0.9753 0.9992

It's a different story for the triangle.  Here's the model:

src/models/triangle.stan
------------------------
parameters {
     double(-1,1) y;
}
model {
     lp__ <- lp__ + log(fmax(0.0,1.0 - fabs(y)));
}
---------------------

The fmax() just makes sure we get -infinity
rather than NaN for probabilities of points
outside of [-1,1].

I have bounded y to be (-1,1), which works just
fine.  If I remove the bound, it doesn't sample
the corners well.

Transformed variable (same conditions):

       0%   2.5%    10%    25%    50%    90%  97.5%   100%
   -0.992 -0.758 -0.522 -0.269  0.008  0.526  0.769  0.954

Untransformed variable (ditto):

       0%   2.5%    10%    25%    50%    90%  97.5%   100%
   -0.858 -0.803 -0.504 -0.301  0.033  0.557  0.746  0.782

The quantiles for the transformed-variable samples are right,
but the untransformed ones are too thin on the tails.

============ bonus section: fmax and fabs() =========================

I used the C++ lib functions fmax() and fabs()
instead of the C++ lib functions because max() and abs()
because the latter have undefined behavior for
floating point (they were originally only for int
types).  Some of the bugs in our distributions were
from using abs() where we should've used fabs().

It's ugly, but the alternative is a layer of
C++-to-Stan function aliasing, which I'd rather stay
away from if I can manage (though with user extensions
and required namespaces in names, I may decide it's
the lesser of two evils at some later point).  The main
reason is that I've always found renaming layers (as in
J2EE) to be very confusing.  The secondary reason is that
it means less coding and hence less doc and less maintenance.

- Bob

Hi,

If you run Wawro's model with something like

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ demo/wawro --data_file=/opt/wawro/
stan/wawro.dump

and read samples.csv into R (code below), the first 18 columns
(corresponding to parameters) have a lot of unique values and the
remaining 50 columns (corresponding to derived parameters) have one
value, zero. I assume it's a bug to not store the derived parameters
but otherwise it's a feature request to store them (or maybe have the
option).

infer them from the order of the parameters.

I have the ``correct'' estimates now.

while the last two are for JAGS.

I am not sure it is worth looking, but report this before
I forgot again.

--
Jiqiang

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] read/write derived params + R interface
messages.body_plain:
Now that I added local variables, the idea
is to print all the derived parameters as well
as the parameters.  It was working, but my latest
patch must've broken it.  We need better tests
around the behavior of the models, not just their
compilability.

Re P.S.  I plan to generate code that'll let
you read the whole thing into R as a list.
How do I specify the header?  If I have a
simple scalar x and a 2-D array y, I'd like to write
a header like:

# x, y[,1], y[,2]

but I can't figure out how to get R to accept
anything like this or manipulate it once it's
written.  So I was thinking I'd just do something
roughly as follows (only getting all the R right):

read_file <- function(path) {
   sample_matrix <-
   as.array(scan(path)),
            dims=c(num_samples,num_params),
            byrow=T);

   y[,1] <- sample_matrix[,1];
   y[,2] <- sample_matrix[,2];

   params <- list(y=y,...);

   return params;
}

The right thing to do would be to generate C++ code
to write directly into R.  But I probably want the
file-based thing, too.

- Bob

On 1/4/12 10:00 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> Hi,
>
> If you run Wawro's model with something like
>
> goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ demo/wawro --data_file=/opt/wawro/
> stan/wawro.dump
>
> and read samples.csv into R (code below), the first 18 columns
> (corresponding to parameters) have a lot of unique values and the
> remaining 50 columns (corresponding to derived parameters) have one

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] undesirable traceplot
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the analysis.

I'm glad the traceplot was bad before it converged
and that running it longer got to the right answers.
They ran a lot of the BUGS examples for a long time.

We can look into what's giving the algorithm a hard
time.

- Bob

On 1/5/12 8:48 AM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> In bugs example vol1/equiv, I had difficulty matching
> results from Stan to those from JAGS, so I look at the
> traceplots.  The traceplots for two variance parameters
> are not good.  After running a longer chain (20000),
> I have the ``correct'' estimates now.
>
> The first two pages of plots are for samples from Stan
> while the last two are for JAGS.
>
> I am not sure it is worth looking, but report this before
> I forgot again.
>
> --
> Jiqiang

OK.

> Re P.S.  I plan to generate code that'll let

I would say that an R function should return an object of class "mcmc"
from the coda library, rather than a list. If you don't want to depend
on the coda library (not really a big deal IMO), then I would say a
data.frame is preferable to a plain list.

>

I was thinking that the parser would make the write_csv function
engrave the parameter names into the first line of the .csv file
automagically with something like this near the top

if(writer__.lines() == 0) {
  // have the parser construct a vector of names called names
  for(unsigned int k_0 = 0; k_0 < dim_names; ++k_0) {
    writer__.write(names[k_0]);
  }
  writer__.newline();
}

Then, inside R you can just call

samples <- read.csv(path, header = TRUE)

at which point samples is a data.frame with column names that could be
converted to something else fairly easily with as.*() functions, e.g.

as.matrix(samples)

as.list(samples)

messages.subject: derived parameter defs & I/O
messages.body_plain:
As things stand, when you write derived parameters,
the code in the derived parameter block is run,
but NOT the code in the model.  Thus if the transforms
are defined in the model, they won't be part of the
output -- the variables will remain zero.

Here's the plan of how things should go.  I could
change this so that the model statements (other than
samples) are also run before output of derived params.

What you need to do is move the derived param definitions
into a block after the declarations.  For example,

WRONG:

   ...
   derived parameters {
       double z_sq;  // declared as derived param
       ...
   }
   model {
       z_sq <- z * z;  // WRONG:  defined in model
       ...
   }

RIGHT:

   derived parameters {
       double z_sq;
       ...
       z_sq <- z * z;  // OK:  defined in derived param block
   }
   model {
       ...
   }

I plan to add some error checking that will actually
make the WRONG line a compile error.  I need to do
this in general so that

   * assignments in derived data only to derived data
     variables

   * assignments in derived params only to derived param vars

   * assignments in derived quantities only to derived quants

I've added truly local variables, too.  So if you want to,
you can do this in a model

   model {
       ...
       for (n in 1:N) {
           double mu; // local var declared at head of statement block
           mu <- alpha * x[n] + beta; // assigned within block scope
           y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
       }
       ...
    }

   * local vars can be assigned only within the block of statements
     in which they were defined

There is already error handling in place for this.

Now I could change this behavior so that the model
code is run again (I set up the generator so I can
drop the sampling statements, which won't need to be
run).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
You've hit two things on my to-do list for the release.

I'm actually surprised running parallel processes
didn't work.  There shouldn't be any interference.
I don't know much about how for-loops work in the shell.

1.  Allow random seeds to be specified per chain.

2.  Allow real multi-threading.  It doesn't look like
you need this.

I don't know a portable way to run multi-threading easily.

I've tested thread local variables for the auto-dif
stack (the only issue for multi-threading in our code),
and it gives you about a 20% performance hit in my testing,
but will work.  It's not really configurable in the current
design, but I'd like to change that.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Local vars probably don't work yet.  It shouldn't
take long to get the code generated.

Backward compatibility with people's programming
idioms is hard and not necessarily desirable.

I'm hoping that sensible error messages will go
a long way to mitigating the transition problems.

I think the main problem with the Wawro model is
that I changed the Stan language after we built
the first version!  (Though I wasn't actually planning
to allow the derived parameters to be monitored --
I always thought of them as locals -- the params are
what goes into HMC and actually gets sampled -- but
then there's code duplication issues recreating them
on the outside ...)

The plan is to store all the parameters and
derived parameters.  The only issue is that the
derived parameter transforms need to be defined in
the derived parameter block rather than in the model.

I was thinking of a "local" or "nuisance" label for
param declarations which would prevent their being
written.  But I decided it'd be better to just have
a convention of writing all params, derived params
and derived quantities.  Those that a user doesn't
want to write can be declared as local.  There's
no such thing as a local parameter, though -- they
always all get written --- they're what's getting
sampled in HMC/NUTS and we need to monitor convergence.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I just want to mention that at least in some bugs examples,
I guess storing the derived parameters is not necessary.
In some cases, it is convenient to declare an array of
parameters, and use the loop from 1 to N in the model
declaration.  So I have ended up using something like this

parameters {
   int N;
   double alpha[N-1];
}

derived parameters {
  double yaalpha[N];
  yaalpha[1] <- 0;
  for (i in 2:N) yaalpha[i] <- alpha[i - 1];
}

In this case, monitoring yaalpha[1] can be problematic.

--
Jiqiang

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: derived parameter defs & I/O
messages.body_plain:
On 1/5/12 2:32 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> I just want to mention that at least in some bugs examples,
> I guess storing the derived parameters is not necessary.

If a parameter doesn't need to be stored, it can
be moved from being a derived parameter to being
a local parameter in the model without changing the
behavior of the model.

> In some cases, it is convenient to declare an array of
> parameters, and use the loop from 1 to N in the model
> declaration.  So I have ended up using something like this
>
> parameters {
>     int N;
>     double alpha[N-1];
> }
>
> derived parameters {
>    double yaalpha[N];
>    yaalpha[1] <- 0;
>    for (i in 2:N) yaalpha[i] <- alpha[i - 1];
> }
>
> In this case, monitoring yaalpha[1] can be problematic.

The issue here's the semantics of "monitor",
which really involves two things:

1.  save/write:  we'll do this for all parameters
and derived parameters.

2.  convergence monitor:  we'll do this for all
parameters.

It would be convenient for external convergence monitoring
to also write the unconstrained version of the parameter
vector as seen by HMC.  The parameter view to clients is
the constrained version (e.g., deviations are positive,
simplexes have K constrained dimensions, etc.)

- Bob

messages.subject: more mailing lists?
messages.body_plain:
I'm now seeing the wisdom of theano's layout

   http://deeplearning.net/software/theano/#community

   Register to theano-announce if you want to be kept informed on
   important change on theano(low volume).

   Register and post to theano-users if you want to talk to all Theano
   users.

   Register and post to theano-dev if you want to talk to the developers.

   Register to theano-github if you want to receive an email for all
   changes to the GitHub repository.

   Register to theano-buildbot if you want to receive our daily buildbot
   email.

   Ask/view questions/answers at metaoptimize/qa/tags/theano (itï¿½s like
   stack overflow for machine learning)

   We try to stay organized with Theanoï¿½s Trac

   Come visit us in Montreal! Most of the developers are students in the
   LISA group at the University of Montreal.

That'd be our existing two groups

   stan-users
   stan-dev

and two more:

   stan-announce
   stan-buildbot

I have a feeling most of the stan-users registrees might be more
likely candidates for stan-announce.

Our equiv of "Theano's Trac" would be our issue tracker, and we
could even invite folks to visit us at Columbia!

I'm not sure about metaoptimize -- I'd almost rather just
use stackoverflow itself.  But we could suggest a tag for several
of these setups.  The problem is that I don't want to have to
monitor several locations for questions.

- Bob

messages.subject: agrad::var as smart pointer
messages.body_plain:
These C++ design books are enlightening.

It turns out that our stan::agrad::var class is an
instance of what's known as a "smart pointer".  That
is, it holds onto a pointer, has value (copy) semantics,
and manages its pointer resources internally.

I added two functions that are conventional for
smart pointers, operator*() and operator->(), so
that the following test now passes:

typedef stan::agrad::var AVAR;

TEST(AgradAgrad, smart_ptrs) {
   AVAR a = 2.0;
   EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(2.0, (*a).val_); // operator*
   EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(2.0, a->val_);   // operator->

   EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(2.0,(*a.vi_).val_);
   EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(2.0,a.vi_->val_);
}

As you can see, operator*() returns
the same as *(a.vi_) and a-> acts
like a.vi_->.

This'll simplify all the vari definitions.

- Bob

messages.subject: implementing multiple methods in stan/nuts
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Matt3.  I had some thoughts following up on our conversation yesterday  (For the others:  The background is that HMC and basic Nuts have problems with distributions that have tails that decline faster than Gaussian or slower than exponential. For example, the right tail of the log-transformed gamma distribution falls off like exp(-exp(x)), and the tail of the t falls off like x^(-alpha).  HMC fails with both of these, but slice sampling works ok in either case, also Girolami's adaptive HMC works.)

Matt has a couple ideas for altering Nuts so that the step size can vary dynamically along the Hamiltonian paths.  Girolami's method is too slow and doesn't scale well but Matt has a couple of clever shortcut ideas that look like they could do it.  The plus side of these algorithms is that they work in examples such as the triangular dist, the log-transformed gamma, and the t.  The minus sign is that they add complications and they slow everything down.

In our conversation yesterday, I suggested perhaps some triage approach, where Stan would start with basic Nuts, then we'd compute some diagnostic statistic (Matt3 suggested monitoring the 3rd derivative of the energy function, which would detect the too-short tails but not the too-long tails, so maybe we'd need another diagnostic for that), and if it reported problems the algortihm would automatically switch to the more elaborate algorithm.  This would have the advantage of running the simpler faster algorithm when that's all we need (which I suspect will be a lot of the models that are commonly fit in Bugs etc).

But then I had another idea, which is to compute the diagnostic after each powering-up of Nuts.  That is, Nuts does 1,2,4,8,16,etc. leapfrog steps.  We could, for example, have Nuts start by doing the first 8 or 16 using the basic method, then switching to the more complicated algorithm after that?

This doesn't sound quite right either but maybe some version of this adaptation is possible.  I understand the need to preserve detailed balance but I'm thinking there should be some way of using this automatic third derivative calculation to only uncork the more alaborate algorighm when it's needed?

A

messages.body_plain:
1.  The point of Matt's log-transformed gamma example is that you can indeed get hyper-short tails even after the natural transofrmation.

2.  I don't know that we need to implement Gibbs---for one thing, that will require additional model-reading ability--but it could make sense to implement Metropolis.

3.  One crude way of solving the short-tail problem is to alternate iterations of Nuts and Metropolis.  I think this will solve the triangle and log-gamma distributions.  It won't solve the Cauchy distribution, though.

A

messages.subject: multivariate normal density
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

In src/stan/prob/distributions/multi_normal.hpp , there are two
parameterizations of the multivariate normal distribution. The first
takes mu and Sigma, while the second takes mu and L, where L is a
Cholesky factor of Sigma. I believe it would be much better --- faster
and more numerically accurate --- if the first simply calculated L and
called the second.

There are three slow and inaccurate things in the first, more
textbookish, implementation. First, the check_cov_matrix() function
checks Sigma for squareness, symmetry, and sufficient positivity of
its eigenvalues. Second, the determinant of Sigma is calculated.
Third, the inverse of Sigma is calculated. Neither the determinant nor
the inverse calculation exploit the positive definiteness of Sigma.
Also, if one were going to calculate the eigendecomposition of a
matrix, you would already have the ingredients for the determinant and
the inverse. But the eigendecomposition is worse than the Cholesky
decomposition anyway.

The Cholesky decomposition in Eigen does some checking and has
a .info() method to check whether something went wrong numerically.
So, you could just do Sigma.llt(), verify the .info(), and pass
the .matrixL() to the second implementation of the density.

But, is there any currently any route to the multivariate normal
density that doesn't construct Sigma from the
stan::prob::read_cov_matrix() function? If there is no such route,
then it isn't necessary to check whether Sigma is square, symmetric,
or positive definite. And, I can easily change things so that there is
a way to return L instead of Sigma := L * L.transpose() because L is a
function of the primative parameters that gets calculated anyways. In
which case, we could just call the second multivariate normal density
implementation directly.

I realize we are not overly concerned about performance for a 1.0
release, but the multivariate normal is so common and this looks like
a very low hanging fruit. Is there a more subtle reason for the way
the code is now?

Ben

are now is that I literally just copied the textbook
definitions out and then ran some simple tests.

> implementation. First, the check_cov_matrix() function
> checks Sigma for squareness, symmetry, and sufficient positivity of
> its eigenvalues. Second, the determinant of Sigma is calculated.
> Third, the inverse of Sigma is calculated. Neither the determinant nor
> the inverse calculation exploit the positive definiteness of Sigma.

I hear they're also less numerically stable.

> Also, if one were going to calculate the eigendecomposition of a
> matrix, you would already have the ingredients for the determinant and
> the inverse. But the eigendecomposition is worse than the Cholesky
> decomposition anyway.
>

> a .info() method to check whether something went wrong numerically.
> So, you could just do Sigma.llt(), verify the .info(), and pass
> the .matrixL() to the second implementation of the density.

That's really useful.  We'll just use .info() for error checking.

> But, is there any currently any route to the multivariate normal
> density that doesn't construct Sigma from the
> stan::prob::read_cov_matrix() function?

Yes.  Stan's syntax checker only makes sure
the argument's a matrix.

What I'd really like to be able to do for some
of these complex distributions is to only call
a solver once if the matrix is a constant.

Right now, there's not a good way to parameterize
that in Stan.

What I want is the equivalent of an eager evaluation
at model construct time for constants and a lazy
evaluation for the other arguments.

So with a Normal(y|mu,Sigma), for instance, if
Sigma were a Matrix<double> rather than Matrix<var>,
I'd like to get all the solving monkey business out of
the way up front and then call something like
Normal_Sigma(y|mu).

Taking this idea even further, we'd pull loop-constant
calcs out of loops.  Right now, we're thinking of
vectorizing some common cases by hard coding them,
but it'd be nice to have a way to do it in the language
when performance matters.

> If there is no such route,
> then it isn't necessary to check whether Sigma is square, symmetric,
> or positive definite. And, I can easily change things so that there is
> a way to return L instead of Sigma := L * L.transpose() because L is a
> function of the primative parameters that gets calculated anyways. In
> which case, we could just call the second multivariate normal density
> implementation directly.

That would be a great option to add.

> I realize we are not overly concerned about performance for a 1.0
> release, but the multivariate normal is so common and this looks like
> a very low hanging fruit.

This is definitely worth doing.

 > Is there a more subtle reason for the way
> the code is now?

None whatsoever.   Just my own ignorance of (numerical) linear
algebra.

- Bob

Hi Daniel,

On Jan 9, 9:59 pm, Daniel Lee <bear...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> Good points. The answer is that we haven't had the time to go through

> src/test/agrad/distributions/multi_normal_test.cpp

OK, I will soon.

> Regarding the checks, that's something I think we should leave in.
> Perhaps we can work in a lighter check, but I won't make the
> assumption that stan::prob::read_cov_matrix() is the only way this
> function is called.

Perhaps another way to ask the question is whether a parameterized
covariance matrix should ever be allowed to get to the multivariate
normal density evaluation without coming from some sort of a
decomposition that ensures positive definiteness by construction. The
case where Sigma is a constant that Bob alluded to is a different
animal. The only scenario I can think of is if stan ever does
rejection sampling.

But the .llt() method will check that Sigma is square. And I think it
is the case that if Sigma is not symmetric and positive definite up to
some numerical tolerance, then .info() is supposed to indicate a
problem, but this may not be 100% guaranteed. The .ldlt() method is a
bit more reliable, but you have to be careful when using it for
statistical purposes because Eigen uses pivoting. So, I think it would
be okay for the first implementation of the density to do one of these
two Cholesky decompositions, check the .info(), and call the second
implementation.

If there were some reason to do the eigendecomposition, then just do
it inside the density function, use the eigenvalues to calculate the
determinant, and use the reciprocal eigenvalues to calculate the
inverse (rather than calling check_cov_matrix(Sigma),
determinant(Sigma) and inverse(Sigma) separately).

Ben

Another way to restate the issue is: What, if anything, prevents the
user from

0) Declaring a vector in the parameters block called covariances
1) Declaring a matrix in the derived parameters block called Sigma
2) Stuffing these covariances into Sigma with a nested for loop
3) Using that Sigma in a multivariate normal density in the model
block (along with some priors over the covariances)
4) Presuming that stan will magically do something reasonable if a
realization of Sigma were not an admissible covariance matrix.

If the answer is that multi_normal_log() throws a runtime error if
Sigma is inadmissible, then I could see why we need to check Sigma
thoroughly on every iteration. But I think it would be better if this
could be a compile-time error so that multi_normal_log() can be as
fast as possible.

WTFDBUGSD?

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On 1/9/12 11:02 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> Another way to restate the issue is: What, if anything, prevents the
> user from
>
> 0) Declaring a vector in the parameters block called covariances
> 1) Declaring a matrix in the derived parameters block called Sigma
> 2) Stuffing these covariances into Sigma with a nested for loop
> 3) Using that Sigma in a multivariate normal density in the model
> block (along with some priors over the covariances)

Nothing at all.  The following's legal:

----------------------
parameters {
     cov_matrix(5) Sigma;
     ...
}
derived parameters {
     matrix(5,5) Omega;
     for (m in 1:M)
        for (n in 1:N)
           Omega[m,n] = Sigma[m,n];
     ...
}
model {
     y ~ multi_normal(mu,Omega);
}
------------------

(I'm about to rename "derived parameters" to
"transformed parameters".)

You can also replace that nested for loop
with a simple "Omega = Sigma;".

> 4) Presuming that stan will magically do something reasonable if a
> realization of Sigma were not an admissible covariance matrix.

Suppose you assigned to Omega in such a way that
it is not positive definite.  In the code
as written above, the call to multi_normal_log(),
which happens per leapfrog step, will throw
an exception.

If instead you declared Omega as cov_matrix(5), then
there will be a check right after the derived parameters
are calculated which will throw an exception.

>
> If the answer is that multi_normal_log() throws a runtime error if
> Sigma is inadmissible,

Daniel's incorporated Boost error policies, so we can
configure multi_normal_log() to do whatever we want.
We want it to throw an exception.

A sampler can then decide to just treat an exception
like a rejection, or it can abort.

 > then I could see why we need to check Sigma
> thoroughly on every iteration. But I think it would be better if this
> could be a compile-time error so that multi_normal_log() can be as
> fast as possible.

Given the flexibility noted above, we can't check
semantic constraints at compile time.

I suppose we could do something like you're suggesting
if we restrict the operations applied to covariance
matrices to be positive-definiteness preserving.
We can do assignment, we can rescale variances per
dimension -- what else?

It'd be some effort to code as I'd have to push more
information than dimensionality through to the semantic
type checker on the Stan side.

My plan right now (in fact, that's what I sat down
at the computer to do) is:

   program, statement, and expression well-typedness:
     Stan compile time (catch errors before C++)

   data:
     constraints checked on data as it's read in

   transformed data:
     constraints checked after transformed data
     blocks calculates transformed data

   parameters:
     initial values checked as read in
     ?? per leapfrog step (after model statement)
     final values checked per sample during write

   transformed parameters:
     ?? per leapfrog step
     final values checked per sample during write

   local variables:
     can't be declared as constrained, no checks

   derived quantities:
     checked per sample after calculated

   expressions/functions:
     dimensional well-formedness at compile time
     constraints on values checked as functions are applied
        (data read time for transformed data,
         per leapfrog step for transformed params and model,
         per sample for derived quantities)

The checks marked with ?? are the ones that would
really slow things down.

> WTFDBUGSD?

WTF does BUGS do?  It's closed source, so we'd have
to ask.  I think JAGS is using the R density
libs, so probably whatever R does.  I don't know how
configurable that is.

One of the reasons we wrote Stan was because BUGS and JAGS
are not very good with covariance matrix parameters.

We had to write our own density libs so that we could
separately template out each arg for auto-dif.

>
> Ben

- Bob

P.S.  I sort of like top-posting.  Everyone gripes about it, but
       with enough context, I prefer it.  What do you all think?

messages.body_plain:
1.  If the covariance matrix is constant data,
we can just invert it once and call

multi_normal_log(y,mu,Sigma); // Sigma covariance matrix
multi_normal_prec_log(y,mu,Tau); // Tau precision matrix

Then if the precision matrix Tau is data, the right
behavior falls out of the way we're dealing with
constants versus variables -- that is, we drop
the log(det(Tau)) term.

2.  Another inefficiency comes from duplication in
values for symmetric matrices.  It'd be better if
we could take only half a matrix, then use a
self-adjoint view of it (in Eigen's terminology) if we
need to treat it as a full matrix.  The loop would
then simplify to

   for (m in 1:K)
     for (n in m:K)
        ...

We only need to do half (plus K/2) of the assigns.

A big obstacle is the poor interaction of Eigen template
expressions like self-adjoint and our auto-dif.  That could
potentially be addressed, though I'm not exactly sure how
at the moment.

All of this is of course do-able in Stan[C++],
which doesn't have any training wheels.  We can
turn off error checking altogether by configuring
the error policy (at least I think we can -- Daniel?)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: multivariate normal density
messages.body_plain:
Ben's right -- there's no way to tell the
difference between plain old user error in
an ad-hoc covariance matrix construction,
arithmetic issues in the same, and arithmetic
issues in a sequence of ops that's supposed
to maintain positive definiteness (given arbitrary
precision).

If we have operations that are supposed to
maintain positive definiteness, I'd make it those
operations' responsibilities to maintain positive
definiteness.

Matt already added a bit of this fudging to some
of the log/logit calcs.  We don't want our users
to be reduced to the inelegant BUGS/JAGS solution
of:

     x <- max(0,min(1,inv_logit(...)))

It would be useful, at least for the multivariate normal,
to have a simple function:

   double transpose_multiply2(vector x, matrix y) {
       return x.transpose() * y * x;
   }

(I can't think of a good name for this operation -- help?)

For one, it'd minimize promotion of doubles to
auto-dif variables in matrix ops, which would otherwise,
if x is data, involve the promotion of the
row vector x.transpose() and original vector x.

We'd probably need a second version if we went with
the maintain-positive-definiteness guarantee.

When JAGS hits a NaN, it sometimes logs and sometimes
crashes.  I'm not sure what the conditions are.  I'd
guess a limited number of retries then failure.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] parser / forgetting to declare stuff
messages.body_plain:
Could you provide a Stan model that does this?

The compiler should catch undefined variables.  What
I probably did was check for dimensionality match
even before I check for variable well-definedness.

There are three flavors of error:

data { }
derived data {
    double y;
    vector(10) z;

    x[5] <- 2.0; // (1) unknown variable
    y[5] <- 2.0; // (2) known variable, too many indices
    z <- 2.0;    // (3) mismatched LHS and RHS

    y <- 2.0;     // OK
    z[5] <- 2.0;  // OK
}

The check for whether a variable is unknown should happen
before the index test.  The kind of message you saw is
intended for the "too many indices" and "too few indices"
cases.  I should dump out the name of the variable, too.

I need to work on the error messages (it's on the to-do

messages.subject: Re: multivariate normal density
messages.body_plain:
I'd agree that operators should be responsible for maintaining
positive definiteness, but should they trust that the matrix they are
given is positive definite or should they check it? For a function
like

>    double transpose_multiply2(vector x, matrix y) {
>        return x.transpose() * y * x;
>    }

if y is PD, then the result is guaranteed to be positive, but how does
it know that y is PD if a user might do something that calls it on a
matrix they made up? This is why I was wondering if we need some
internal classes like symmetricMatrix or psdMatrix that can be trusted
to be symmetric or PSD because they are instantiated by a responsible
constructor within stan. Then, we can have safer functions that are
defined for a plain Matrix that check once per iteration whether a
matrix that should be symmetric or PSD or whatever, is so.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: multivariate normal density
messages.body_plain:
I conflated multiple issues. Yes,

>    double transpose_multiply2(vector x, matrix y) {
>        return x.transpose() * y * x;
>    }

should exist because it would be used by any elliptical distribution.
Although the above would actually be a subtle compiler error because
x.transpose() * y * x is a 1x1 matrix, whereas the calling function
wants the scalar ( x.transpose() * y * x)[0]. But if it were

>    Matrix<T, dynamic, dynamic> transpose_multiply2(MatrixXd x, Matrix<T, dynamic, dynamic> y) {
>        check_psd(y);

>        return x.transpose() * y * x;
>    }

the resulting matrix would be PSD (up to numerical tolerance) if y is
but neither have any PSD branding. If it were

>    psdMatrix<T, dynamic, dynamic> transpose_multiply2(MatrixXd x, psdMatrix<T, dynamic, dynamic> y) {
>        return y.multiplyonbothsides(x);
>    }

then we don't need to check whether y is PSD but do need the
symmetricMatrix and psdMatrix classes, plus constructors,
documentation, etc.

Ben

 > Can we evaluate the log posterior on iteration 0 with a higher level
 > of scrutiny than subsequent iterations?

Warning: back to Stan-dev.

Yes, that would be easy.  What do you want to scrutinize?

I'm guessing we're just going to have to bail if
it's ever -infinity or NaN.  If we have a bad initial
init, we almost certainly won't be able to move into another
state at all.  It's different after that, in that we can
just keep rejecting.

But we're also monitoring rejection rate, or some approximation
thereof, so we should catch a long string of rejections, too.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: parser / forgetting to declare stuff
messages.body_plain:
I'd say check everything we can think of on iteration 0 and much less
for subsequent iterations. So for iteration 0,

-- Accessing vector / matrix elements all within range
-- Are all pointers non-null
-- Is every data point and parameter finite
-- All derivatives non-zero but finite
-- ...

Also, maybe we could try to extrapolate on iteration 0 whether the
consumption of time, RAM, etc. is going to be reasonable and print
that to stdout.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Re: parser / forgetting to declare stuff
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the suggestions.

Given the flexibility of the language, things
can still go wrong later, but most of the errors
will be in the first iteration, so we could be
more stringent.  I tend to think like an all-or-nothing
computer scientist -- either I can guarantee it's
safe or not.  And we can't really guarantee safety -- the
best we can do is check declared constraints.

The only way to get a null pointer is if a
parameter or derived parameter or local model
variable is used before it is assigned a value.

Positiveness of derivative is a good thing to
check everywhere.  As you move around the space,
you can wind up in bad places if you don't have
the right constraints, etc.

I definitely want to profile with an expected
time-to-completion.  The problem with that for Stan
is that there's a long adaptive burn-in/adaptation (of
step size) phase that's rather different than what
happens later.  And the real big problem is that
the number of steps varies dramatically with step
size, so until we burn-in/adapt, it's hard to estimate
time until completion.

- Bob

messages.subject: array bounds & init checking
messages.body_plain:
There are two places so far that Stan can seg fault (basically
crash out of C from trying to read memory it shouldn't).

1) using a transformed parameter that has only been declared
but not assigned a value, or

2) using out of bounds array indices.

BUGS solves these problems by:

1) making sure every variable is either sampled (a
parameter for us) or assigned (a transformed parameter
or transformed data) exactly once in the code, and

2) calculating array bounds by running the first iteration
of the model.

At the cost of slowing everything down a bit, I could
implement array-bounds checking and defined checking in
the Stan-GM models.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] missing data and stan
messages.body_plain:
Any missing data model in BUGS can be
translated into Stan 1.  I've gone over how to
do it in past e-mails and on Andrew's board
and will include examples in the doc.

The basic idea is to break the vector of data
into missing and non-missing parts and then
duplicate code.  Ugly for the repetitious code,
but it works in general.

The problem with directly translating the BUGS
models is that Stan doesn't allow mixed vectors
of data and parameters.  The types, double and
stan::agrad::var, don't mix.  We can't fix the
value of a parameter given the way HMC works.

After breaking them out, you can put them
back together into a transformed parameter vector
or matrix.  For instance, you might want to do this
if the missing "data" is an entry in a covariance
matrix some of whose entries are known.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: missing data and stan
messages.body_plain:
OK, that is really good. I'll watch the commits for an example of how
to do a model like that.

For the special case of covariance matrices with known entries, I
should probably write a non-ugly dedicated mechanism. In the canoncial
partial correlations framework, fixing the i-j regular correlation
implies a nonlinear constraint (that we would have to solve) on the i-
j CPC and the triangularity of the Jacobian implies that these only
affect "downstream" correlations. Basically, we can just reduce the
number of free (primitive parameters underlying the) CPCs by the
number of constraints on the regular correlations and proceed.
However, it may be the case that for some values of the known and free
parameters, there is no solution for the fixed CPC on the (-1,1)
interval, which we would have to deal with somehow.

Ben

messages.subject: templated RNG in NUTS
messages.body_plain:
I needed to get my hands on the seeded random
number generator (RNG) up in the command.  So
I wanted to construct it there and pass it into
NUTS.  So...

I added a template parameter to NUTS for the
base RNG.  It defaults to the previous hard-wired
value:

     template <typename RNG = boost::mt19937>
     class nuts : public adaptive_sampler { ... };

I changed the constructor to take a base RNG
seeded with the time:

       nuts(mcmc::prob_grad& model,
            double delta = 0.6,
            double epsilon = -1,
            T base_rng = T(std::time(0)))

I use copy semantics for the RNG (well-defined for boost::random)
rather than a reference.

Thus the behavior won't change for clients that didn't set
a random number seed.

But we will need a template arg list, even if it's empty:

       stan::mcmc::nuts<> sampler(model, 0.5, -1);

If we need a constructor with the
random-number seed, I can reinsert one.

- Bob

messages.subject: parallel random number generation
messages.body_plain:
Do we need to worry about this?  Malecki had brought
it up before.

I did some reading and the issues are:

1.  Thread safety.  This isn't an issue for us at
the moment and we could either (a) synchronize, or
(b) use different RNGs in different threads.

2.  Independence.  The problem is that if you have
an int seed, there are only 4G possibile inits.
If you do a fairly large number of chains (on the
order of 100K), there's a good chance two of them
will be the same.

I don't think either's a problem.  But do let me know
if you have more insight than me on this issue.

Given the reparameterization of NUTS, it'll be easy to
plug in Boost's L'Ecuyer RNG.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: parallel random number generation
messages.body_plain:
I believe the main problem is that if you initialize a plain RNG from
the clock time and you start the chains at essentially the same time,
then the chains are not independent,  even if the seeds differ by 1.

A quick and dirty way to mitigate this problem is to take a random
seed independently from /dev/random for each chain. But the rigorous
way is to use the L'Ecuyer RNG.

Ben

we'd be good to go.

Here's a link to the R doc:

It could use better examples.  The "Details" section
makes it clearer what's supposed to happen -- access up to
7 different substreams, each of which is "independent".
But you need to start by providing 7 seeds.  They have
a built-in way to do that, but how's that different than
what I suggested above?  How is L'Ecuyer helping?

Boost doesn't give us that kind of functionality for
L'Ecuyer.  In particular, I don't see how to get out
multiple streams:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_48_0/doc/html/boost/random/ecuyer1988.html

as far as I can see.

messages.subject: Re: parallel random number generation
messages.body_plain:
There's a simple but computer science oriented PDF of the issues
involved here

http://www.cs.berkeley.edu/~mhoemmen/cs194/Tutorials/prng.pdf

that explains things better than I do.

One approach is to "split" a single stream into say 5 parts for 5
chains. I think most of these approaches to deterministic splitting
rather than splitting at (pseudo) random points because if each chain
needs a lot of pseudo-random numbers and you get unlucky and split at
a bad place, then there could be overlap.

My limited understanding is that the L'Ecuyer algorithm in R is that
is it is better than splitting one stream in the sense that it
actually makes different streams.

Now, if boost doesn't support what R supports, then it's a dead end.
Does this link help you

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_48_0/libs/mpi/example/parallel_example.cpp

It seems to be a splitting approach rather than (one of) L'Ecuyer.

A more fundamental question is whether you are intending to have stan
take something like a --number_of_chains=5 argument, where the user
would call stan once and stan would spawn 5 threads, one for each
chain. In that case, maybe some form of splitting would work. However,
if you are intending to have stan take something like a --random_seed
argument, where the user would call stan 5 times, then it is up to the
user to supply numbers that do the splitting as appropriately as
possible.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: parallel random number generation
messages.body_plain:
You can get a little more explanation by executing

vignette("parallel")

in R 2.14.x, especially section 6. I think a big part of L'Ecuyer is
the elegant leaping mechanism. But it also says something I didn't
know, which is that equal width splits are not necessarily optimal.

As far as I can tell, boost just hasn't put a lot of effort into
parallel PRNGs. Are we wedded to boost or just BSD? If the latter,
maybe have a look at http://numbercrunch.de/trng/ .

Ben

messages.subject: finally building on Windows
messages.body_plain:
On 1/13/12 4:49 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
 > For test/gm/parser:
 > 1) g++ 4.7.0 experimental runs the test at -O3! Yay!

Thanks for going in today and checking, Daniel.
Great news that it's finally working

To bring everyone else up to date, we haven't
been able to get the Stan parser (the thing
that reads the Stan files and generates a data
structure corresponding to the program) to build
under Windows.  Daniel and I have spent dozens of
hours working on the code, searching, trying different
compilers, etc., all to no avail.

I wrote a couple of messages to the developer mailing
list for Boost, built them a standalone test, and a
couple of their developers got back to me -- the
bottom-line is that it still won't compile with
-O0, but it will compile with -O3, which is fine
for production.  Go figure (though you'll have to
be a template yoga master to figure this one out).

With -O0 under GNU, it either blows out memory in the
compile, generates a suspect .o file, or crashes the GNU
assembler (the assemblers converts some abstract representation
of the program into more concrete machine code per platform).
The Boost guys looked into it and concluded it's a bug
in the Windows GNU assembler.

One of Boost's taglines is "torturing compilers since
1999".

- Bob

The config file's there in the repository.
You're running it from the right location, too.
As far as I can tell, none of the makefile cleans
clean it out.

There are syntax errors in many of the distribution
formulas in the doc.  They were too complex to debug,
so I just yanked them (out of inv_gamma, beta and
multi_normal).  You can find them back in revision 525.

As a reminder, you can use valid LaTeX between \f$ ... \f$
in Doxygen.  I add one formula at a time and remake the

messages.subject_clean: clang / g++ on my Debian laptop
messages.body_plain:
The problem of me not being able to build stan on Debian with clang
can (almost) be solved by installing the development files for clang.
Linux distributions are in the habit of splitting up libraries so that
people can install only the parts that they need. In my case, I needed
to do

apt-get install libeigen-dev

so that the proper *mmintrin.h files will be found before falling back
to the problematic ones in g++.

I added a sentence to this effect in README.txt .

However, it then could not find uintptr_t, so I added

#include<stdint.h>

to src/stan/memory/stack_alloc.hpp , which was actually mixed up in
the previous commit that added another parameterization of the beta
density (I hate subversion).

At that point, with clang++, make demo/gm works. However, make all
segfaults consistently on one of the tests

test/agrad/error_handling --gtest_output="xml:test/agrad/
error_handling.xml"
Running main() from gtest_main.cc
[==========] Running 15 tests from 1 test case.
[----------] Global test environment set-up.
[----------] 15 tests from AgradDistributionsErrorHandling
[ RUN      ] AgradDistributionsErrorHandling.CheckNotNanDefaultPolicy
[       OK ] AgradDistributionsErrorHandling.CheckNotNanDefaultPolicy
(0 ms)
[ RUN      ] AgradDistributionsErrorHandling.CheckNotNanErrnoPolicy
Segmentation fault
make: *** [test/agrad/error_handling] Error 139

I don't know much about this Policy business so someone else should
have a look. On a related note, my implementation of the
aforementioned beta density is just

      beta_ls_log(const T_y& y, const T_mu& mu, const T_theta& theta,
const Policy& = Policy()) {
        T_mu alpha = mu * theta;
        T_mu beta = (1.0 - mu) * theta;
        return beta_log(y, alpha, beta, Policy());
      }

The compiler didn't like me just passing Policy and insisted on
passing Policy(), so maybe I am doing something wrong.

Ben

Just to talk about what I have on Ubuntu regarding clang.

I am using an old version of Ubuntu, which does not have clang3+.
So I have to build myself.  However, the problem for clang++ is that
it could not find the libstdc++ header files.  Even I tried to follow
the following instruction (which I think it is a bit ambiguous) on
http://clang.llvm.org/get_started.html

6. If you intend to work on Clang C++ support, you may need to
tell it how to find your C++ standard library headers.
If Clang cannot find your system libstdc++ headers,
please follow these instructions:

'gcc -v -x c++ /dev/null -fsyntax-only' to get the path.

Look for the comment "FIXME: temporary hack: hard-coded paths"
in clang/lib/Frontend/InitHeaderSearch.cpp and change the lines
below to include that path.

Currently, I could built clan++ luckily so that it could find
the header file.  For example, it tells me it would find header
files as the follow examples shows.

$ clang++ -v a.cc
...
clang -cc1 version 3.1 based upon LLVM 3.1svn default target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
ignoring nonexistent directory "/include"
#include "..." search starts here:
#include <...> search starts here:
 /opt/gcc/include/c++/4.6.3
 /opt/gcc/include/c++/4.6.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
 /opt/gcc/include/c++/4.6.3/backward
 /usr/local/include
 /opt/llvm/bin/../lib/clang/3.1/include
 /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu
 /usr/include
End of search list.
...

This is a tricky little pattern here.  Bottom line is
that Policy is a (template) type and Policy() is a
constructed instance of type Policy.

Note that there is no variable name in that last argument.
This is intentional.  We're only using Policy() for the
type inference!  If we ever need an actual Policy instance,
we just construct one in the body of the function using
Policy().

This is apparently a very common pattern with policies.

Daniel went ahead and used the C++11 feature of allowing
default parameter types in function templates (they were
always allowed in class templates).

- Bob

not all of our users are like Ben and able to
pull up gdb and start tracing the error through C++.

At the cost of some potential slowdown, I can
have the behavior be that if someone tries to
access a variable that hasn't been initialized,
it can be:

A.  set to 0

This is the behavior of a member variable, not the
behavior of a local variable, which is undefined
before it's initialized.

B.  throw a (configurable) error

This would at least let people know why their
program crashed, though I won't be able to give
much diagnostic info on the variable in the model
as that's lost by the time you get to var.

 >          Eigen::Matrix<typename promote_args<T_y,T_loc>::type, Dynamic,

You need to add T_y to the promote_args list for half,
as in:

Eigen::Matrix<typename promote_args<T_covar,T_y,T_loc,>::type,
               Dynamic, 1> half = = multiply(L_inv,diff);

That's because the element type of diff is promote_args<T_y,T_loc>
and the element type of L_inv is T_covar.

All the direct calls like half.dot(half) should be OK
because there's just a single type involved.

If you haven't gotten it to work, can you either send
me the code via e-mail (or just go ahead and check it in),
or send me the full error dump (assuming it's not 100 pages).

messages.subject_clean: multivar norm problem's in Eigen triangularView()
messages.body_plain:
Good news now (bad at the end).  I fixed
the template syntax problem in multi_normal.
The key issue is that this won't compile:

   template <typename T>
   void
   foo(Matrix<T,Dynamic,Dynamic>& L) {
     L.triangularView<Eigen::Lower>();
   }

Because of the . and < in the template, it turns
out you need to nudge the C++ parser a bit with
a hint (otherwise "L.triangularView" is parsed as
a member object and "<" as a binary operator):

   template <typename T>
   void
   foo2(Matrix<T,Dynamic,Dynamic>& L) {
     L.template triangularView<Eigen::Lower>();
   }

Who knew?

I fixed multi_normal.hpp so that it compiles and
made a few other changes.

I renamed the second function to "multi_normal_cholesky_log".

I also replaced the template expression triangular view
argument with a regular old matrix, only the lower-triangular
portion of which will be used.  Views aren't really meant
to be passed as arguments.

Two bits of bad news, though:

Compiling crashes clang++ on my Mac.

~/stan>clang++ -v
clang version 2.9 (tags/RELEASE_29/final)
Target: x86_64-apple-darwin10
Thread model: posix

2.  It's not getting the value in the test.

I checked that everything's getting passed right
and the inverse and diffs are right.  I don't
actually know the right formula, so I hope Ben
can debug it from here.

- Bob

  function(X) {

messages.subject: Re: implicit functions and stan
messages.body_plain:
It's obvious for explicit functions that stan can handle the
derivatives with AD.

It's not obvious but true and really cool that stan can produce a
derivative with AD in situations where we can only numerically
approximate the function. So, I am pretty sure we could upgrade the
parser to handle something like

parameters {
  double theta;
}
derived parameters {

  double(0,1) rho;
  rho <- 0.5;
  rho <- numerically_solve(rho, g(rho | theta, x), TOLERANCE);
}

But numerically_solve() is going to propagate a ton of AD calculations
that aren't conceptually necessary because we can calculate the
derivative of rho wrt theta from the ratio of the derivatives of g(rho
| theta, x) wrt rho and theta. So, it is almost like we need to tell
stan to skip the AD calculations inside numerically_solve() and
afterward graft the implicit derivative onto the tree in the right
place. That sounds theoretically possible, but I don't know if we have
the flexibility to do that yet.

Ben

We can code anything for which we can code
g(x) and its derivative g'(x).  It doesn't matter
if g(x) is solved numerically by iteration and
g'(x) is computed analytically.  In fact, we'll
run into this case with cumulative densities.

The issue must be can we somehow define a function
g(...) in Stan and then automatically solve it
and automatically differentiate it.  I don't see
why not, though there's nothing like that in there
now.  Matt's been talking about adding solvers
that could themselves be based on auto-dif.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: writing output CSV with headers
messages.body_plain:
help(as.mcmc, package = "coda")

will show you the documentation, but is basically just "pass it a
matrix or data.frame with columns as parameters".

If you use R2WinBUGS to *estimate* a model via WinBUGS, then they have
some parsing of the BUGS output into what is called a bugs.array that
has 3 dimensions for parameters, chains, and draws. But, if you are
not using WinBUGS, then you have to construct your own bugs.array to
analyze it with Andrew's plotting functions in the R2WinBUGS package.

Andrew would probably want a function that takes Stan output from
multiple chains and makes it into a bugs.array, but I think most
people would prefer to use the coda package.

In both cases, we can supplement these objects with information on the
burnin, thinning rate, etc., which isn't knowable from samples.csv,
but should be easy when calling from rstan.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: implicit functions and stan
messages.body_plain:
Right. Prerequisites for this feature would be

-- a C++ function to numerically solve an equation in one variable
-- a way for the parser to get the equation to be solved from
the .stan file to the numerical solver.

But, it would be even better if we could short-circuit the AD.

Say we have an explicit log-density function

f(y | theta, rho)

but with a constraint on the parameters

rho^5 - rho == theta

from which we get g(rho | theta) = rho^5 - rho - theta .

It is impossible for the user to write rho as an explicit function of
theta:

parameters {
  double theta;
}
derived parameters {
  double rho;

  rho <- ???
}

but the user could write something like this

implicitly defined parameters {
  double rho;

  rho <- 1.0;
  rho <- numerically_solve(rho, rho^5 - rho - theta);
}

The way stan is now, there would be a lot of AD going on inside
numerically_solve(). But humans know that for any rho that satisfies
the constraint,

[d rho] / [d theta] = 1 / (5 * rho^4 - 1)

via the implicit function theorem. In other words, I think the brute
force approach of propagating AD through a while loop would create a
big branch on the tree that ultimately accounts for [d rho] / [d
theta] when we already know its formula but can't evaluate it until we
get rho.

So, can we program stan to not create a big branch of AD to calculate
[d rho] / [d theta] while numerically_solve() is finding rho, but
instead wait until rho is found, and then put the value of 1 / (5 *
rho^4 - 1) wherever it needs to go?

Ben

> We can code anything for which we can code
> g(x) and its derivative g'(x).  It doesn't matter
> if g(x) is solved numerically by iteration and

> g(...) in Stan and then automatically solve it
> and automatically differentiate it.  I don't see
> why not, though there's nothing like that in there
> now.  Matt's been talking about adding solvers
> that could themselves be based on auto-dif.
>
> - Bob

> On 1/16/12 11:31 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
> > It's obvious for explicit functions that stan can handle the
> > derivatives with AD.

> > It's not obvious but true and really cool that stan can produce a
> > derivative with AD in situations where we can only numerically
> > approximate the function. So, I am pretty sure we could upgrade the
> > parser to handle something like
>
> > parameters {
> >    double theta;
> > }
> > derived parameters {
> >    double(0,1) rho;
> >    rho<- 0.5;
> >    rho<- numerically_solve(rho, g(rho | theta, x), TOLERANCE);

One advice in the literature is to only auto-dif

    example, which implicitly defines a function f()

b) auto-dif the bits of the definition of f()

c) use the implicit function theorem to propagate
    derivatives of the function.

messages.subject: Re: implicit functions and stan
messages.body_plain:
One perhaps motivating example is the so-called "generalized lambda
distribution".

http://www.stat.ucl.ac.be/ISdidactique/Rhelp/library/Davies/html/Gld.html

The GLD cannot express its PDF or its CDF in closed form. Rather, the
distribution is defined by the inverse of the CDF, say Q(p | lambda).

To indirectly evaluate the density, f(y | lambda), you first have to
numerically find the value of the CDF, p = F(y | lambda), such that
Q(p | lambda) == y.

Given p, the value of the density is known to be something like 1 /
Q'(p | lambda).

So, that is an example where in order for the user to model something
(basically anything continuous and unimodal) with a GLD, stan would
have to internally do some efficient numeric solving, implicit
differentiation, etc.

Since that is internal, maybe that is an easier starting point than
the more general case where the user (often economists) have some
arbitrary constraint they need to impose on the parameters, like the
rho^5 - rho == theta example, where we would have to parse an
arbitrary implicit function in order to pass to the numeric solver.

Ben

messages.subject: constraints & renamed cmd options
messages.body_plain:
I just committed a major patch to the way
variable constraints work in Stan (for everything
but parameters).

1.  All variables allow constraints other than
     local variables.

2.  Data and transformed data constraints are enforced
     after data is read in.

3.  Transformed parameters checked as sample is written.

4.  Generated quantities checked as sample is written.

5.  Testing constraints is done through cassert (at least
     for now) and can be turned off for extra speed like
     other asserts during compilation.

I also changed the names of command-line parameters.
These are now available from the compiled command via
--help, which now prints:

~/stan>demo/temp --help

Compiled Stan Graphical Model Command

USAGE:  demo/temp [options]

OPTIONS:

   --help              Display this information

   --data=<file>       Read data from specified dump-format file
                         (required if model declares data)

   --seed=<int>        Set random number generation seed

   --inits=<file>      Use initial values from specialized file
                           (default is random initialization)

   --iter=<+int>       Total number of iterations, including burn in
                           (default = 2000)

   --burnin=<+int>     Discard the specified number of initial samples
                           (default = iter / 2)

   --thin=<+int>       Period between saved samples after burn in
                           (default = max(1, floor(iter - burnin) / 1000))

   --delta=<+float>    Initial parameter for NUTS step-size tuning.
                           (default = 0.5)

   --samples=<file>    File into which samples are written.
                           (default = samples.csv)

   --append_samples    Append samples to existing samples file if it exists
                           (default erases existing samples file before
writing)

   --refresh=<+int>    Period between samples producing progress output
                           (default = max(1,iter/200))
- Bob

messages.subject: accessing elements of Eigen types
messages.body_plain:
As explained here

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/QuickRefPage.html

in the section on Basic Matrix Manipulation of Eigen types,

y[i] // checks to make sure i is not outside range
y(i) // checks range unless NDEBUG is defined
y(i,j) // checks range unless NDEBUG is defined

Our makefile passes -DNDEBUG, but you can take that out temporarily to
check whether a new function has range errors. And we should probably
have Jenkins not pass -DNDEBUG ever.

But the big problem is that there are a ton of instances in stan's C++
files that use the bracket notation, meaning that we waste wall time
range checking every little thing. I grepped 547 instances, but some
of those are false positives. We probably should fix all of them.

Ben

messages.subject: Proposal for ColVector, etc.
messages.body_plain:
In stan, there are a lot of functions whose arguments are something
like

const Matrix<T_loc,Dynamic,1>& mu

This is less readable, hard to type, more prone to bugs, etc. than I
think it could be, especially considering that we don't use any of the
fixed size functionality in Eigen.

For example, I have discovered (repeatedly) that if you write a test
with something like

Eigen::VectorXd mu(5)
mu.setZero();

and pass that, you get a compiler error even though VectorXd is a
typedef for Matrix<double,Dynamic,1>. Similarly,

Eigen::MatrixXd mu(5,1);
mu.setZero();

and pass that, you get a compiler error because MatrixXd is a typedef
for Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic>.

What I would like to write in function definitions is just

const ColVector<T_loc>& mu
