messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Proposal for ColVector, etc.
messages.body_plain:
It's a bit more complicated because Eigen's leaning on
C++ "concepts", not inheritance.  I'll comment inline.

On 1/17/12 2:34 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> In stan, there are a lot of functions whose arguments are something
> like
>
> const Matrix<T_loc,Dynamic,1>&  mu
>
> This is less readable, hard to type, more prone to bugs, etc. than I
> think it could be, especially considering that we don't use any of the
> fixed size functionality in Eigen.

The place we used fixed sizes is for vectors and row-vectors,
as in the 1 above.  Eigen specializes the Matrix template
for when one of the arguments is a fixed-size 1.

BUT, there are three more template arguments with defaults,
_Options, _MaxRows, and _MaxCols.

> For example, I have discovered (repeatedly) that if you write a test
> with something like
>
> Eigen::VectorXd mu(5)
> mu.setZero();
>
> and pass that, you get a compiler error even though VectorXd is a
> typedef for Matrix<double,Dynamic,1>.

Not quite.  It's

typedef VectorX< double > 	VectorXd;

with

VectorX<T>

being its own template specialization of VectorBase.  See:

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/1/namespaceEigen.html#32b84ab7510b90d7b1e1fcd510163265

and

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/1/classEigen_1_1VectorX.html

It may look like VectorX extends Matrix, but it's an
illusion.  It just acts like a matrix in template
expressions (it's what they call a "concept" in C++
and the whole idea's so foreign from a Java perspective
that it keeps tripping me up).

One of the confusing things is that Matrix itself has
a templated constructor that'll accept anything that
acts enough like a matrix to provide values.

So it's not quite so easy to do what you want to do
directly.

We might be able to replace all the vector usages with
explicit VectorX operations.  But it may be easier.

 > Similarly,
>
> Eigen::MatrixXd mu(5,1);
> mu.setZero();
>
> and pass that, you get a compiler error because MatrixXd is a typedef
> for Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic>.
>
> What I would like to write in function definitions is just
>
> const ColVector<T_loc>&  mu
>
> I don't think it is possible to make ColVector a typedef and still
> pass a template parameter like T_loc.

Here's where using traits classes could help.

template <typename T>
struct EigenType {
     typedef T scalar;
     typedef Matrix<T,Dynamic,Dynamic> matrix;
     typedef Matrix<T,Dynamic,1> vector;
     typedef Matrix<T,1,Dynamic> row_vector;
};

Now you can use things like EigenType<T>::matrix
for a matrix of type T.

     typename EigenType<T>::scalar
     typename EigenType<T>::matrix
     typename EigenType<T>::vector
     typename EigenType<T>::row_vector

for types.  In your example, that'd be:

     const EigenType<T_loc>::vector& mu;

It might even require a typename first.

It's not great, but it's arguably clearer
and more abstracted than:

     const Matrix<T_loc,Dynamic,1>& mu;

The nice part about this is that we know it'd work without
any compiler gymnastics.

There are already typedefs (matrix_d, matrix_v, etc.)
when the type is known in the code.

 > But I think the following is
> possible with  little cost:
>
> -- Make the ColVector class inherit from the Matrix class

This should probably be one of the Vector classes.

> -- Make "default" template parameters of Dynamic and 1 for
> RowsAtCompileTime and ColsAtCompileTime respectively
> -- Have the constructor throw an error if RowsAtCompileTime and
> ColsAtCompileTime are anything other than Dynamic and 1 respectively

This would presumably be a compile-time error.

> And the opposite for RowVector although I don't think we would use
> that much. Maybe also StanMatrix<type>  where both RowsAtCompileTime
> and ColsAtCompileTime "default" to Dynamic and the constructor throws
> an error on anything but Dynamic?
>
> Thoughts? I'm not totally sure under the c++11 standard whether an
> inherited class can add default template parameters when the parent
> class leaves those template parameters undefaulted, but hopefully it
> does.

Apparently, you can.  My design book recommends against changing
defaults in subclasses, though.

- Bob

messages.subject: "derived" should now be "transformed" in models
messages.body_plain:
I changed the keyword "derived" to "transformed"
in the models.  I replaced in all the models after
a fairly cursory check that it wouldn't cause
damage, but there may be some cleaning up to do in
some of the models.  I also re-organized the
non-BUGS models a bit.

So now a Stan program looks like:

data { ... }
transformed data { ... }
parameters { ... }
transformed parameters { ... }
model { ... }
generated quantities { ... }

with everything but the model block optional.

Every variable other than a local variable can have
constraints, and the constraints are tested:

data, transformed data:  data read time, before sampling

parameters: test on inits if inits provided

transformed parameters:  test on write (NOT every leapfrog step)

generated quantities:  test on write (only generated as sample is written)

- Bob

messages.subject: beta
messages.body_plain:
For starters, there is a bit of potential confusion in beta_log() in

src/maths/special_functions.hpp

refers to the  log of the beta(a,b) *function*, whereas beta_log() in

src/stan/prob/distributions/beta_distribution.hpp

refers to the log of the beta(y, alpha, beta) *density*. So even
though they have different signatures, maybe we should change one of
the names?

Also, the textbook version of the beta distribution is usually defined
in terms of two shape parameters, which is how Bob and / or Daniel did
it for stan. However, when modeling a proportion with covariates and
an inverse link function, it is customary to parameterize the beta
distribution in terms of the mean (mu) and a precision parameter
(phi), where

mu := alpha / (alpha + beta)
phi := alpha + beta

See section 2 of http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/betareg/vignettes/betareg.pdf
for details.

I have added wrappers for these mu / phi parameterizations with names
beta_ls_log() and beta_binomial_ls_log() (with "ls" for location-
scale). The question I have is how is the user supposed to access them
in the .stan file that simply references "the" beta density? Of
course, users could implement the mu / phi parameterizations
themselves with local shape parameters in the model block:

double alpha
double beta

for(i in 1:I) {
  mu <- inv_logit(something);
  alpha <- mu * phi
  beta <- (1.0 -  mu) * phi;
  y[i] ~ beta(y[i], alpha, beta);
}

But how can we save the user the trouble of converting from mu / phi
to alpha / beta? Does it need to say something like

y[i] ~ beta_ls(y[i], mu, phi)

Ben

going before I commit using clang++ (2.9 still)
and -O0.  And there are actually fewer includes.
I found and eliminated lots of useless ones.

Ah, 18 minutes end to end.  But it works.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: constraints & renamed cmd options
messages.body_plain:
Some issues with these command options. First, --seed is currently
allowed to be a string, which causes the seed to be 0, which
nonetheless says is "randomly generated". My guess is that this is due
to the "characters are ints" paradigm of C-based languages and
afflicts many of the options. E.g.

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan-svn$ demo/ds --data=/opt/wawro/third/
ds.dump --iter=4 --seed="foobar"
NUTS
sample_file=samples.csv
num_iterations=4
num_burnin=2
num_thin=1
delta=0.5
random seed=0 (randomly generated)
iteration=1 burning in
iteration=2 burning in
iteration=3 saving
iteration=4 saving

Also, I think if a --seed is supplied by the user, it should say
random seed = X (user supplied) rather than random seed = X (randomly
generated).

Can we make it so that if --refresh is 0, then it doesn't print
anything to stdout? Also, no matter what you set --refresh to
currently, it prints every iteration.

Ben

messages.subject: maths::beta_log now maths::lbeta; prob::beta_ls_log removed (for now)
messages.subject_clean: maths::beta_log now maths::lbeta; prob::beta_ls_log removed (for now)
messages.body_plain:
I just pushed through the lbeta name change.

Which led me to the new beta_ls parameterization.
It needs a fair bit of work.  So I just removed
it (and commented out tests).  If we need to bring
it back, it was last seen in:

     revision 561

I feel bad for yanking it, but I'd rather wait until
a stable version 1 to put more work on Daniel's and
my plate for error checking code, testing, etc.
But feel free, Ben, to go back in and add all of this
stuff yourself if you really want beta_ls that
badly.

Here's an outline of fixes needed.

The original version was:

     template <bool propto = false,
               typename T_y, typename T_mu, typename T_theta,
               class Policy = policy<> >
     inline typename promote_args<T_y,T_mu,T_theta>::type
     beta_ls_log(const T_y& y, const T_mu& mu, const T_theta& theta,
		const Policy& = Policy()) {
       T_mu alpha = mu * theta;
       T_mu beta = (1.0 - mu) * theta;
       return beta_log(y, alpha, beta, Policy());
     }

1.  It needs error checks actually on the
mu and theta params.  We want to guarantee
mu is between 0 and 1 and that theta is positive
and do it with feedback as to which distribution was
called.  If the products aren't right, we'll currently
get errors reported as originating in beta_log,
not beta_ls_log, which will confuse the users.

2.  I named types for the kinds of variables, not
the actual variable (other than for outcome y),
so it's (T_loc mu, T_scale sigma), not (T_mu mu, T_sigma sigma).
I suppose it could be T_mean instead of T_loc -- it seems
odd to call mu a location here.

The extra naming gives people some hint as to what the
parameter is.  (This made me realize that the variables
for the standard beta parameterization should be T_scale_success
and T_scale_failure rather than T_alpha and T_beta.)

3.   The types declared for locals alpha and beta need
promotions as they involve T_mu and T_theta:

       typename promote_args<T_mu,T_theta>::type
       alpha = mu * theta;
       typename promote_args<T_mu,T_theta>::type
       beta = (1.0 - mu) * theta;

So that must mean there aren't unit tests for the
appropriate types in place.

An easier alternative would be to just drop them
into the beta_log call directly -- then the types all
get auto-computed from the operations.

- Bob

This model's really confusing (like Wawro's!).

like this (more efficient than adding a derived parameter,

messages.body_plain:
As I coded that example, before looking at the details, I could talk about some
that might help.

The feature that JAGS dose not support but Openbugs does is cycles.
This happened again in vol3/jama example, in which actually I only writes
the following now:

# http://www.openbugs.info/Examples/Jama.html
# Jama River Valley Ecuador - Radiocarbon calibration with phase information

# It turns out that the model specified in OpenBUGS
# has *cycles*, which is not support by Stan (and JAGS).
# In section `Directed cycles` of JAGS manual, it writes
#
# Directed cycles are forbidden in JAGS. There are two important instances
# where directed
# cycles are used in BUGS.
# * Defining autoregressive priors
# * Defining ordered priors

So my understanding it that in BUGS, we can specify model, for example,

## a bi-variate normal for (x1, x2)'
## mu <- c(2, 3);
## Sigma <- matrix(c(40, 10, 10, 60), ncol = 2)
## (x1, x2)' ~ mnorm(mu, Sigma)

model {
  x1 ~ dnorm(mu1, tau1);
  mu1 <- 2 + (x2 - 3) / 6;
  tau1 <- 3 / 115;
  x2 ~ dnorm(mu2, tau2);
  mu2 <- 3 + (x1 - 2) / 4;
  tau2 <- 2 / 115;
}

In Stan, this model would be like
parameters {
  double x1;
  double x2;
}
model {
   x1 ~ normal(2 + (x2 - 3) / 6, sqrt(115 / 3));
   x2 ~ normal(3 + (x1 - 2) / 4, sqrt(115 / 2));
}

However, this would be problematic in Stan as Stan does not check if there is any cycle.
And this get *directly* translated into a logposterior as
normal(2 + (x2 - 3) / 6, sqrt(115 / 3)) * normal(3 + (x1 - 2) / 4, sqrt(115 / 2)),
which is not what we want.

Actually, when we did the Wawro's example, I have noticed that and pointed out that
there are cycles in the model specification.  Back then, I did not how
stan parse the model.  I am not sure that is a problem.

--
Jiqiang

In revision 598 I have committed pineapple_ice.stan, which attempts to
replicate the (thankfully, somewhat simpler) parameterization of the
ice model at

www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/documentation/exampVol2/node14.html#SECTION000122000000000000000 <http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/documentation/exampVol2/node14.html#SECTION000122000000000000000>

This parameterization does not have a directed cycle, but it does have
a redundancy where a positive scale parameter (sigma) multiplies a
vector of random intercepts.

If I specify

double(0,) sigma;

stan does not run very well. If it is lucky, it will escape the burnin
period but seems to not converge and yields odd results.

If I cheat a bit and specify

double(0.05,) sigma;

stan runs a lot better and the posterior mean for sigma is a little
more than 0.05, which is in line with the posterior mean of sigma on
page 31 of

http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/winbugs/Vol2.pdf

However, our posterior log Risk Ratios run from -1.43 to 1.06, whereas
theirs run from -1.08 to 1.06, even when I do half a million
iterations.

Although there is a possibility that WinBUGS didn't converge, we've
done it with 350K iterations.

So, it seems that there are a few more things to iron out with this
example.

Ben

messages.subject: "cycles" in Stan graphical models (re: BUGS Ice)
messages.subject_clean: "cycles" in Stan graphical models (re: BUGS Ice)
messages.body_plain:
Stan's parser allows cycles.  But it's up to you
to make sure the probabilities are correct.  For
instance, you can write:

   y ~ normal(x,1);
   x ~ normal(y,1);

and Stan won't complain.  It'll get compiled to

   lp__ += normal_log(y,x,1);
   lp__ += normal_log(x,y,1);

This is a complete Stan model specifiying joint
probability:

   p(x,y) = normal(x|y,1) * normal(y|x,1)

Probably not what we want unless we're hacking an
MI model directly into Stan.

The problem BUGS/JAGS have with cycles conceptually is
that they treat multivariate variable nodes as nodes
of the graph rather than the elements of the vectors.
So if they had:

   x[1] ~ normal(0,1);
   for (n in 2:N)
       x[n] ~ normal(0.5 * x[n-1],1);

They'd think of that as a cycle from x to x because
the variable x shows up on the left-hand and right-hand
sides of the looped sampling.

But the actual random variables are x[1], x[2], ...
and there's no cycle there.

Writing the above kind of thing is totally kosher in
Stan and leads to the right log probability.

- Bob

from anywhere in the mess in the top right corner. It is only
classified as a "cycle" by JAGS because the parameters are all
contained in the same vector named beta and JAGS does not distinguish
among elements of beta.

www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/documentation/exampVol2/node14.html#iceSigfig <http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/documentation/exampVol2/node14.html#iceSigfig>

the question of why pineapple_ice hangs during burnin if sigma is not

On 1/27/12 12:03 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
...

> But, Stan cannot do models with an undirected graph? Like
>
> www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/documentation/exampVol2/node14.html#iceSigfig <http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/documentation/exampVol2/node14.html#iceSigfig>

Stan should be able to handle anything for which you
can:

a.  code up the log probability function, and

b.  transform all variables to be unconstrained.

Although we don't support undirected graphical models
directly, you can just write out their log probabilities
directly in Stan.

That's what BUGS did in its model.  You just need
to be careful you get a proper density (up to a constant).

There are conceptual problems with other BUGS models, like
ordinal logit.  To get ordered points c[1] and
c[2], they write something tha also looks circular:

   c[1] ~ normal(0,1) I(,c[2]);
   c[2] ~ normal(0,1) I(c[1],);

This implies an ill-formed density

   p(c) = normal(c[1] | 0, 1) / (1 - pnorm(c[2]|0,1))
        * normal(c[2] | 0, 1) / pnorm(c[1]|0,1)

but is OK for sampling using Gibbs as the
conditionals are correct.

What you really need in the model spec
is something like the way you'd write the "same"
thing in Stan:

   c[1] ~ normal(0,1)
   c[2] ~ normal(0,1) I(c[1],)

This provides a proper density.

BUGS can't handle this version, because there's a chance
you'll sample c[1] from a point above c[2] without
the constraint.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I think this is not a correct way of specifying this model. I guess it somehow works in BUGS because they're only ever considering one variable at a time. (Although it seems like you have to exploit some really weird "features" of BUGS to get it to work.) But in general it's by no means true that the joint probability of a bunch of variables is proportional to the product of the conditional probabilities of those variables. For example, the conditional probability of β_1 should be
p(β_1|β_-1) = N(β_1; 2*β_2 - β_3, 1)
but in the model as specified in Stan I think it'll be something like
p(β_1|β_-1) = N(β_1; 2*β_2 - β_3 + 2/5*β_2 - 1/6*β_3, 1/(1+1/5+1/6)).
The issue is that there are a bunch of terms that are being double-counted.

So maybe it's not so surprising that it's giving weird results?

Matt

graphs.  If it were, every undirected graph with at least
one edge would have a cycle.  Usually it means that
there is a non-empty, non-repeating path of edges from a
node back to itself.

 > In other words, if I have say

>

I think I'm seeing the confusion here.

There's a whole literature on "undirected graphical
models", which are used for Markov random fields.
(See, e.g., Koller's book "Probabilisitc Graphical
Models"), or the Wikipedia entry:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_random_field

I now realize that BUGS is using the terminology
from both graph theory and graphical models in
exactly the non-standard way Jiqiang thought.
That is, they're using

   { a --- b }

as shorthand for

   { a --> b, a <-- b }

> By the way, I take Bob's explanation with a gain of salt.  Because

I would, too, if JAGS allows that model.  What kind of cycle
does JAGS NOT allow?

> interested.

Is there a way to write down the log posterior you
are interested in up to an additive constant?
If so, it should be possible to just code it directly in
Stan.  The Stan statement

    a ~ foo(theta);

is just shorthand for:

    lp__ += foo_log(a,theta);

You don't have to worry about how it gets computed, as
they seem to be doing in BUGS/JAGS with their conditionals.

Of course, as Matt pointed out, you aren't guaranteed a proper
joint model by writing out a product of conditionals (I'm
sure you guys are used to this discussion from MI!).

> I would quote from p3057 of Lunn et al (2009)
> http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/bayescomputation/lunnbugswithcomments.pdf

>     by a single node in the graph with complex internal structureï¿½if all

>     internal nodes can be updated
>     together, then the internal structure is unimportant for the
>     purposes of performing the encompassing
>     Gibbs scheme

I see what they're getting at for sampling.  You do the
same thing for computing potential functions in MRFs,
looking at maximal cliques (largest fully connected subgraphs).

Grouping isn't relevant for Stan -- it does all params at
the same time like Metropolis.  I'm not sure I understand what
Lunn et al. mean in terms of modeling, but I suspect it's
what Jiqiang said, using an undirected edge as shorthand for
both directed edges.

- Bob

On Jan 27, 1:48 pm, Jiqiang Guo <guoj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I am trying to find the corresponding model in BUGS for pineapple and
> vanilla later.

I said it wrong earlier. This is what I think is true at approximately
2:15 PM (subject to change at 2:16 PM or later):

Classic BUGS lists 3 ways to do the "same" model here:

www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/documentation/exampVol2/node12.html <http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/documentation/exampVol2/node12.html>

The corresponding text files are available here:

http://www.stat.uiowa.edu/ftp/woodwort/BUGSXmpl/Classic%20Examples/EXAMPLES/VOL2/ICE/

The first ("Autoregressive smoothing of relative risks") is
implemented in ICEAR.BUG are corresponds to the example in JAGS.

The second ("An undirected model using an intrinsic prior for the
random effects") is implemented in ICECARSG.BUG and corresponds to
pineapple_ice.

The third ("An intrinsic prior with a hyperparameter") is implemented
in ICECAR.BUG and (in theory) corresponds to both the example in
WinBUGS and vanilla_ice.

When I said that the WinBUGS example and BUGS example refer to the
same graph, that was wrong. The WinBUGS example corresponds to this
graph

http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/documentation/exampVol2/node15.html#iceCARfig

which they refer to as "undirected", presumably because there are no
arrows linking the betas (only arrows linking tau to the betas).

They also have a table of posterior estimates from the three versions
of the model. However, the results in the third column differ from
those given in the WinBUGS manual, from the other two columns, and
from the original article. For vanilla_ice, Stan gets close on sigma
but not on the logRRs.

Hopefully that addresses a part of the confusion.

Ben

> conditionals does not give you the joint to which those conditionals

Thanks for clarifying -- there are two issues here.

One is that we want a properly specified model,
and multiplying a bunch of conditionals might
not do that.

Two is what Matt just said, and what I was
trying to get at with the ordinal logit cutpoint
example.  The only cases I know where the product
of conditionals give you the joint is when there
is independence.  So directly using the BUGS formulation
can lead you astray as they can get away with conditionals
specified up to a proportion.

Bottom line (literally):  for Stan, the only thing
that matters is getting the correct log posterior (or log joint)
up to a proportion.

- Bob

So it's not a subtle question of the way that pineapple_ice or vanilla_ice handles tau, it's that there simply is no correct way to specify the ice model this way in Stan.

messages.subject: log likelihood? joint? posterior? reported in output
messages.subject_clean: log likelihood? joint? posterior? reported in output
messages.body_plain:
Andrew was suggesting that we add the log probability
to our output to support some * information criteria
calcs.

It looked like WAIC needed a log LIKELIHOOD, not
a log posterior or log joint.  There's NOT a good
way to get at that in Stan, because Stan doesn't know
what the user is thinking of as data.

I could start thinking about how we can generate
code to calculate a log likelihood using the data
specification as the data (but this doesn't seem to
be what we want in the mixture indicator variable
case, as mixture indicators need to be specified as
parameters; on the other hand, we could sum out
the mixture indicator in this case in the program).

The problem is that for SAMPLING, a Stan model only
requires the log posterior up to a proportion.  That's
the only thing that's going to be straightforward to
calculate and report.

For instance, the fully specified model

     parameters { double(0,1) theta; }
     model { theta ~ beta(1,1); }

and the underspecified model

     parameters { double(0,1) theta; }
     model { }

behave the same way with respect to sampling,
because beta_log(theta|1,1) = constant.

But there's no way for the second program to recover
the normalized log joint or log posterior, even though it'll
sample just fine.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
We hit another snag in the discrete
distributions.  Right now, we have the
moral equivalent (modulo templates) of:

double poisson_log(unsigned int, double lambda);

The problem is that if someone passes an int
into this, it'll get converted to an unsigned int
and we'll never catch problems arising from it
being negative.

I propose changing all our distributions to take
a signed long and do the checks.

Anyone see any problems with that?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] variable errors crashing NUTS
messages.body_plain:
It looks like the issue is that there's a finite but huge variance parameter that, when exponentiated, returns inf. This is the result of a too-large stepsize. The correct behavior would be to return -inf, which will cause NUTS to stop and kick the step size down a notches.

I feel like we already had a long discussion about this, but I think our options are
1. Reconfigure the distributions to accept infinite scale parameters and return -inf.
2. Reconfigure leapfrog() to catch exceptions and return -inf.
3. Reconfigure NUTS to catch exceptions and treat them as -inf.

#2 is the cleanest, fastest fix, and arguably makes sense. If exceptions are always the result of parameters leaving their acceptable ranges, then an equivalent model to the one we're trying to fit is one that says that p(parameters outside range)=0. But if there's another kind of exception that can occur when you call grad_log_prob() then we'll ignore it, possibly at our peril.

Thoughts?

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] log likelihood? joint? posterior? reported in output
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] log likelihood? joint? posterior? reported in output
messages.body_plain:
Hi--I talked more with Aki today.  What I learned:

1.  I'm more sure than ever that we should be computing Waic.  I don't think there's any need for us to compute DIC or any of the others.

2.  Computing Waic is more effort than I thought, because we not only need the log likelihood, we also need the log likelihood for each data point.  Which means that we need to save it as a vector for each iteration, or else go
back and compute it in post-processing at the end.

3.  There are further complciations for models such as binomial where we want individual 0/1 data to be the "data points" for Waic, but the data might be coded as y-out-of-n.

I have thoughts on how best to do this, we can discuss further on Wed.

See you
A

On Jan 27, 2012, at 3:15 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> Andrew was suggesting that we add the log probability
> to our output to support some * information criteria
> calcs.
>
> It looked like WAIC needed a log LIKELIHOOD, not
> a log posterior or log joint.  There's NOT a good
> way to get at that in Stan, because Stan doesn't know
> what the user is thinking of as data.
>
> I could start thinking about how we can generate
> code to calculate a log likelihood using the data
> specification as the data (but this doesn't seem to
> be what we want in the mixture indicator variable
> case, as mixture indicators need to be specified as
> parameters; on the other hand, we could sum out
> the mixture indicator in this case in the program).
>
> The problem is that for SAMPLING, a Stan model only
> requires the log posterior up to a proportion.  That's
> the only thing that's going to be straightforward to
> calculate and report.
>
> For instance, the fully specified model
>
>    parameters { double(0,1) theta; }
>    model { theta ~ beta(1,1); }
>
> and the underspecified model
>
>    parameters { double(0,1) theta; }
>    model { }
>
> behave the same way with respect to sampling,
> because beta_log(theta|1,1) = constant.
>
> But there's no way for the second program to recover
> the normalized log joint or log posterior, even though it'll
> sample just fine.
>
> - Bob

multivariate normal with mean vector zero and a known, very weird,
precision matrix. So, I would need to implement that, which we had
talked about before a little bit.

Do you want a multi_normal_log() whose signature includes a matrix of
doubles rather than a templated matrix or do you want a function with
a different name like multi_normal_log_known_precision()? Also, in
this case, the precision matrix happens to be singular (thus it's an
improper prior) so it *can't* allow propto be true; the
log(det(Sigma)) part would be -Inf. What do you want to do about that?
I would lean toward making a multi_normal_log_improper() function that
ignores the constant always.

Ben

probability function, whereas propto=true includes
only terms containing at least one stan::agrad::var.

The precision matrix will be involved in two terms,
the log(det(Tau)), which we wouldn't evaluate if Tau
was made up of doubles, and the product term with location (mu)
and outcome (y) vectors, which gets evaluated unless the outcome
and both parameters are constant.

What seems to be needed is an "improper" flag
that turns off the check for singularity.  But then
there's still the issue of how to pass flags from
Stan to configure the error-checking on a
call-by-call basis.

One way to go would be as Ben suggests, splitting out
the functions, and using names like:

   multi_normal_precision_improper_log()

The "_log" needs to go last so that you can refer to
the prefix in stan, as in:

    y ~ multi_normal_precision_improper(mu,Tau);

On the other hand, maybe we could add constants to Stan
representing error-checking policies, so that you could
write

    y ~ multi_normal_precision(mu,Tau,IMPROPER);

and the IMPROPER would get translated to an error policy
in C++ and passed to the multi_normal_precision function.

But this is problematic in that we only want to turn off
checks for the precision matrix -- we'd still check that
none of the mu or y were NaN and the mu were finite.

Speaking of this latter decision, Matt argued that
outcome y and location mu should be treated symmetrically,
as they're symmetric terms in the probability function.

Boost throws exceptions if mu is infinite when it
constructs a normal_distro(mu,sigma) (Boost doesn't do
multivariate).  I thought this made sense, because
a normal_distro(mu,sigma) will always returns 0
probability.

On the other hand, if you have a finite mu and positive
finite sigma, then normal_distro(y|mu,sigma) returns
0.  So I also see where Boost's coming from.

The question is, what should we do?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Yes, I meant propto has to (at least in effect) be true when the
precision matrix is singular.

Another possibility for the case where the precision matrix is known
is to precalculate the log determinant, pass it to the function, and
have the function check to see whether it is Inf. In other words, even
if the precision matrix is invertible and the user wants to normalize,
we don't want the function to be recalculating the determinant every
time the function is called anyway.

Relatedly, if the precision matrix is known, I think we would want to
precalculate its 3-factor Cholesky decomposition, Tau = LDL', set U :=
D^(1/2) * L', and pass U rather than Tau. This would save flops inside
the density function, which would basically just be dotself(U.template
triangularView<Eigen::Upper>() * (y - mu)).

So, I don't think we need a version that takes the whole Tau, but the
rest of Bob's questions remain. Also, maybe now is a good time to
reconsider whether we need a  CovMatrix class, which could have
attributes like CheckMe, IsPSD, IsPD, IsInverted, LogDeterminant,
CholeskyFactorization, etc. That way the multi_normal_log() functions
could rely more on polymorphing and have the inside of the function
figure out what calculations it needs to do and what calculations it
can avoid by looking at the attributes.

Ben

slower and risks them messing up log_det_Tau somehow.

> > So, I don't think we need a version that takes the whole Tau, but the

> > can avoid by looking at the attributes.

>
> I've been designing everything with a much more
> functional than object orientation.  It's much
> simpler conceptually as there's no pre-conditions
> or post-conditions in an object's state to maintain.

I don't mind functional. I even tolerate R, which is dysfunctional.
But I do kind of like the way the Matrix package in R does object-
orientation. And it is so difficult to get a covariance matrix right
that maybe it should be treated differently.

> I don't see how to maintain these states given
> the flexibility of Eigen matrice's operator[],
> which returns a REFERNENCE to an element:
>
>     Matrix<T,...>
>
>     T& operator[](size_t n) { ... }
>
> If someone gets such a reference and changes it,
> we can't guarantee any of our checks like isInverted
> or isPosDef or whatever still hold.

In the CovMatrix class in my head, there would be constructors that
would take parameters and output a CovMatrix with the various flags
set. But I can't think of a great reason why some rogue function
should subsequently be changing its elements before the posterior is
evaluated. I might even overload [] and () to throw errors. But if
there were some reason why a function should be changing its elements,
then I would say it is that function's responsibility to set CheckMe
to true so that downstream functions know to go through all the
checks.

Maybe I haven't emphasized the following enough:

-- There are a small number of ways to construct a covariance matrix
that guarantee it will be positive definite
-- And there are a great many ways of constructing a covariance matrix
that do not have a snowball's chance in hell of being positive
definite in all 1000 (or even 3) iterations. The subset of positive
definite matrices within the set of symmetric matrices with positive
diagonal elements is just too small.

So, although we probably can't absolutely prevent the following from
happening:

parameters {
  double covariances[K * (K - 1) / 2 + K];
}
transformed parameters {
  double Sigma[K,K];
  int count;

  count <- 1;
  for (i in 1:K) {
    for (j in i:K) {
      Sigma[i,j] <- covariances[count];
      Sigma[j,i] <- Sigma[i,j]
      count <- count + 1;
    }
}

We need to do everything we can to discourage the user from doing that
because Sigma will not be positive definite in the vast majority of
the iterations. Users should be using convenience functions in
their .stan files like makeLKJ(), makeAR1(), etc. that output valid
covariance matrices. And when those functions are used, we need some
way of indicating that the density should not check Sigma.

The downside is that maybe in the future somebody invents some cool
way of constructing a positive definite covariance matrix that a user
wants to use but isn't implemented in Stan. In that case, they would
have to do it themselves within the .stan file. But I would almost
rather them email a feature request.

Ben

I do kind of like the design of the Matrix package in R (as opposed to
the matrix that is in the base R package, which is basically just a
vector of numbers with a dimensions attribute). You can see its design
for a correlation matrix, for example, with

library(Matrix)
help("corMatrix-class")

A corMatrix has a slot (attribute) called "factors", which is a list
that caches any matrix factorizations like Cholesky and so forth. So
when some high-level operation (like det()) is done to a corMatrix,
the low-level internals are free to carry that out via the Cholesky
factor.

Ben

> On Jan 29, 1:02 pm, Bob Carpenter<c...@alias-i.com>  wrote:
>> On 1/29/12 2:13 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>>> I am sure there are use cases for a parameterized Tau. In fact, I
>>> think Andrew sent me a paper about a distribution for precision
>>> matrices. But I in the case below:
>>
>>>> We could also use this exact same strategy
>>>> if Sigma were a parameter -- just replace
>>>> "data" with "parameters" and "transformed data"
>>>> with "transformed parameters".  Better yet, use
>>>> a local, as in:
>>
>>>>      parameters {
>>>>          cov_matrix(K) Sigma;
>>>>      }
>>>>      model {
>>>>          cov_matrix(K) Tau;
>>>>          double log_det_Tau;
>>
>>>>          Tau<- inverse(Sigma);
>>>>          log_det_Tau<- log(determinant(Tau));
>>>>          for (n in 1:N)
>>>>              y[n] ~ multi_normal_prec_det(mu,Tau,log_det_Tau);
>>>>      }
>>
>>> Why wouldn't the user just pass Sigma to multi_normal()? This way is
>>> slower and risks them messing up log_det_Tau somehow.
>>
>> With Sigma, you need to do all the solving business.  Once
>> you have the precision matrix Tau and log(det(Tau)) it's
>> just multiply/add.  You'd probably want to Cholesky factor
>> it, which you can also do in Stan.
>
> That makes sense iff Sigma were known, but in this case where Sigma is
> parameterized, why not pass Sigma to multi_normal() so that it can do
> solve(Sigma) and det(Sigma) in a fast and safe way?

Because you have to do the same solve N times.
An alternative is to vectorize, and write:

  y ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);

for vector y.  Then multi_normal_log does the same unfolding
inside its loop.  If the mu are determined by regressions,
then we also need to allow passing in a sequence of mu
vectors.

   for (n in 1:N)

       y[n] ~ normal(alpha + beta * x[n], sigma);

with alpha, beta and x[n] simple scalars, turns into

   y ~ normal(alpha + beta * x, sigma);

where y is a vector, x is a vector and alpha and
beta are still scalars, with the expression defined so that

   (alpha + beta * x)[n]
     = alpha + beta * x[n].

so that the whole is equivalent to the original statement
looping over the N.

So far, we've only done this for the regular normal,
and even then, we haven't allowed varying means.  It'll
be a much bigger saving with covariance matrices.

>> Are you suggesting we extend Eigen with a CovMatrix class?
>
> Maybe. I think eventually Eigen will probably extend itself with all
> kinds of structured matrices, but that is not on their agenda right
> now.

Doug Bates and some other folks have been pushing
things like symmetric matrix and easier handling
of positive definiteness

> So, we could "extend" Eigen's Matrix class (and possibly deal
> with the consequences if and when Eigen makes its own CovMatrix class)
> or we could make a totally new class called CovMatrix that "embeds"
> one or more Eigen Matrices as private attributes so that Stan can
> pretty much keep the same API even if Eigen changes in major ways.

I was thinking of whether we'd just do something
in Stan's compiled language, whether we'd try to
do something with a nice C++ API to build into our
matrix class, or whether we'd just do something with
Stan's own modeling language.

Either way, it makes sense to me to extend Matrix.
After all, a CovMatrix is a Matrix.  That lets us apply
all of the usual operators to it.  But given C++'s semantics,
that'd really want us to allow the assignment and
access referent operators.  If it doesn't extend Matrix,
we'll have a ton of work to do defining all the operators
for it.  But then maybe it won't have many.

These kinds of extensions seem to be on Eigen's agenda,
just not highly prioritized.  They're willing to help
with high-level design advice, but need someone to code
and test.

We already plan to go down this road in the near future.
Eigen needs someone to push through all the heterogeneous
operator traits (so that you could multiply a Matrix<var,...>
and a Matrix<double,...>).  That's what we need for much more
efficient matrix auto-diff operations.  Right now, we're
coding around their expressions and have to over-promote
doubles to auto-dif variables, which is costly in terms of
both time and memory.

Currently, Eigen has an example for Matrix<complex,...> and
Matrix<double,...>, but it's hard coded for those types.
That opens the way to an intermediate possibility where we
just follow what they did for complex rather than trying to
generalize all their matrix and operator traits.

- Bob

You made the ops clear in the previous messages, and
they make a lot of sense.  What's nice is that
they'll automatically handle the kind of lifting of
operations out of loops I was talking about in the
last message (at the cost of a very inexpensive cache
check and without requiring the programmer to do
it themselves in Stan, which is doable now, but both
error prone and ugly).

Implementing a Matrix itself may be hard to do
consistently given Eigen's use of the
curiously recurring template pattern and the way
the types get lost after expression assignment.

Eigen's LLT and LDLT classes have the kind of design
Ben's talking about.  They take a matrix in their
constructors, and allow access to the factors through a
method.  They even have a kind of update function, but I
don't think they maintain a full cache-like behavior.
So we could follow that design and I think implement
everything Ben's been suggesting.

All in all, this should be doable in a way that's
natural enough that we could contribute it to Eigen.

- Bob

Aha! Now I see. Yes, we should definitely avoid recalculating an
inverse or a determinant. And, we should try to avoid making users
write optimized .stan files. Ideally, they should just write readable
(and correct) .stan files and Stan should figure out how to do it
fast.

With covariance matrices (more so than other parameters), numerical
algorithms need "the" covariance matrix in various forms. Sometimes
--- but rarely --- you need the literal, textbookish, KxK form,
sometimes you need the SelfAdjointView, sometimes you need a
correlation matrix and standard deviations, sometimes you need a
Cholesky factor, sometimes you need the inverse, etc. And on top of
that, you don't want to store more than you need or being doing the
same autodiff twice, so you have various storeage schemes, dense vs.
sparse, etc. All of that would seem to argue for making a CovMatrix
class (extending Matrix is fine with me) that is capable of
implementing all this but mostly hides the implementation.

Since Doug already went down this road for the Matrix library in R,
I'm sure we could coordinate with him on how best to do it with Eigen.

Ben

No, I'm not talking about anything as difficult as pulling out conditionals for Gibbs.  What will be needed is (a) to flag the terms in the log-joint that correspond to the data model, and (b) separate the n different pieces corresponding to the n data points, thus saving a vector of contributions to the log-density.  This will require further information to be passed to Stan.  Alternatively, we could kluge it by just adding another line in Stan to compute the vector of contirbutions to the log-density.  That would be ugly because it would require writing the "likelihood" part of the model twice, but for the models we've been considering (which have trivial Gaussian, binomial, etc. likelihoods and all the complexity is in the hierarchical prior), it would be easy enough to do.

>
>> 3.  There are further complciations for models such as binomial where we want individual 0/1 data to be the "data points" for Waic, but the data might be coded as y-out-of-n.
>>
>> I have thoughts on how best to do this, we can discuss further on Wed.
>
> What about truly multivariate outcomes like
> multivariate normal?

This depends on the model, but I suppose the usual setting would be a (non-square) matrix of data, n by k, which would be considered as n observattions, each of which is a vector of length k.  So for Waic we'd need to be saving n log-lik numbers for each iteration (or going back and computing n log-liks on the saved iterations, in a post-processing step).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] implementing Waic in Stan
messages.body_plain:
It's easy enough to mark some of the variables
as what you and Jennifer called "modeled data".

   data { int N; }
   modeled data { double y[N]; }
   parameters { double mu; double sigma; }
   model {
       for (n in 1:N)  y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
   }

The problem is that the likelihood terms for these aren't
as clear in Stan models as they are in BUGS (where
they're always on the left-hand side of a ~).  For
instance, with the vectorized operations we were
considering earlier for efficiency, the model would
look like:

   model { y ~ vectorized_normal(mu,sigma); }

and the function vectorized_normal(...) wouldn't even
have an individual term for the likelihood of an individual
outcome y[n] because it only computes the terms involving
sigma once.

This is different than having a vector y drawn
from a multivariate normal, which looks the same, but
apparently leads to only a single data point from
the WAIC perspective:

    model { y ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma); }

In Stan, users can also write out the probability terms
themselves without using ~.  And if we have things
like subroutines, it'll hide sampling details like
for the vectorized_normal example.

It'll probably be easier to talk about this at the
board on Wednesday.

- Bob
